title: Article 12: Definition of 'State'
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: Definition of State, Fundamental Rights, Government of India, Parliament, Local Authorities, Other Authorities, Instrumentality or Agency of State
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Definition of 'State' for Fundamental Rights Enforcement under Part III.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
In this Part, unless the context otherwise requires, 'the State' includes the Government and Parliament of India and the Government and the Legislature of each of the States and all local or other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India.

LEGAL ANALYSIS AND SCOPE:
Article 12 defines the entity against which fundamental rights guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution can be enforced. The term 'State' encompasses four distinct tiers: (1) The Central Executive and Parliament of India; (2) The State Executives and Legislatures; (3) Local authorities such as Municipalities, Panchayats, District Boards, and Port Trusts (as defined under Section 3(31) of the General Clauses Act, 1897); and (4) 'Other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India'. Through expansive constitutional interpretation in landmark judgments like Sukhdev Singh v. Bhagatram, Ramana Dayaram Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India (1979), and Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib Sehravardi (1981), the Supreme Court laid down the cumulative 'deep and pervasive state control' test. Under this doctrine, statutory corporations, government-owned companies, and registered societies (such as CSIR, FCI, and ONGC) qualify as instrumentalities or agencies of the State, making their administrative, regulatory, and commercial actions subject to writ jurisdiction and fundamental rights scrutiny under Articles 14, 19, and 21.

title: Article 13: Laws Inconsistent with or in Derogation of Fundamental Rights
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: Judicial review, void laws, pre-constitutional laws, post-constitutional laws, doctrine of severability, doctrine of eclipse, constitutional amendments
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Foundation of Judicial Review and Constitutional Invalidity of Inconsistent Laws.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
13(1) All laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution, in so far as they are inconsistent with the provisions of this Part, shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void.
13(2) The State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by this Part and any law made in contravention of this clause shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void.
13(3) In this article, unless the context otherwise requires, 'law' includes any Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usages having in the territory of India the force of law.
13(4) Nothing in this article shall apply to any amendment of this Constitution made under article 368.

LEGAL ANALYSIS AND DOCTRINES:
Article 13 serves as the primary constitutional vehicle for judicial review in India. It establishes the supremacy of Fundamental Rights over both pre-constitutional statutes (Clause 1) and post-constitutional enactments (Clause 2). The Supreme Court developed crucial constitutional doctrines around Article 13: (a) The Doctrine of Severability (AK Gopalan, RMDC)—if valid statutory provisions can be separated from invalid ones, only the offending portion is void; (b) The Doctrine of Eclipse (Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of MP)—pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with fundamental rights do not become dead letters, but remain dormant (eclipsed) until a constitutional amendment removes the shadow; and (c) The Doctrine of Waiver (Basheshar Nath v. CIT)—citizens cannot waive their Fundamental Rights because they are established as constitutional public policy. The historic debate between Article 13(2) and Article 368 regarding whether a constitutional amendment is a 'law' was reconciled in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), establishing that while amendments are constituent power, they cannot abrogate the basic structure.

title: Article 14: Equality Before Law & Equal Protection of the Laws
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: Right to Equality, Equality before law, Equal protection of laws, Reasonable classification, Non-arbitrariness, Rule of law, Manifest arbitrariness
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Universal Right to Equality, Reasonable Classification, and Anti-Arbitrariness.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.

LEGAL ANALYSIS AND DOCTRINAL TESTS:
Article 14 combines two foundational concepts: (1) 'Equality before the law', derived from the English Common Law Rule of Law (Dicey), a negative concept establishing that no person is above the law and all classes are equally subject to ordinary jurisdiction; and (2) 'Equal protection of the laws', derived from the 14th Amendment of the US Constitution, a positive concept mandating equal treatment under equal circumstances. The interpretation of Article 14 has evolved through two distinct doctrinal eras:
1. Traditional Reasonable Classification Doctrine (State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar, 1952): Classification is valid if (a) it is founded on intelligible differentia distinguishing persons or things grouped together from others left out, and (b) the differentia has a rational nexus to the legislative object sought to be achieved.
2. Dynamic Non-Arbitrariness Doctrine (E.P. Royappa, Maneka Gandhi, Ajay Hasia): Equality is dynamic and antithetical to arbitrariness. State action that is arbitrary, whimsical, or devoid of reason violates Article 14 per se.
3. Doctrine of Manifest Arbitrariness (Shayara Bano v. Union of India, 2017): Plenary legislation can be struck down under Article 14 if it is capricious, irrational, lacks determining principle, or is excessive and disproportionate.

title: Article 15: Prohibition of Discrimination on Grounds of Religion, Race, Caste, Sex or Place of Birth
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: Non-discrimination, affirmative action, special provisions for women and children, socially and educationally backward classes, EWS reservations
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Specific Guarantee Against Discrimination and Affirmative Action.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
15(1) The State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them.
15(2) No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition regarding access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, or use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads, and places of public resort maintained wholly or partly out of State funds or dedicated to the use of the general public.
15(3) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any special provision for women and children.
15(4) Special provision for advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes (SEBC) or SC/ST (added by 1st Amendment, 1951).
15(5) Special provision for admission to educational institutions, including private institutions whether aided or unaided (added by 93rd Amendment, 2005).
15(6) Special provision for economically weaker sections (EWS) up to 10% (added by 103rd Amendment, 2019).

LEGAL ANALYSIS:
Article 15 is a specific facet of Article 14's general guarantee of equality. Crucially, the presence of the word 'only' in Article 15(1) signifies that if discrimination is based on other relevant criteria in addition to sex, caste, or religion (e.g., physical capacity, economic hardship), the measure does not violate Article 15(1). Clauses (3), (4), (5), and (6) are not exceptions to the equality principle, but substantive equality mechanisms enabling protective discrimination for marginalized demographics (Indra Sawhney, Janhit Abhiyan).

title: Article 16: Equality of Opportunity in Matters of Public Employment
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: Public employment, reservations, backward classes, creamy layer, 50% ceiling rule, carry forward rule, promotions, EWS
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Equality in Public Employment and Constitutional Framework for Reservations.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
16(1) Equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State.
16(2) Prohibition of discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence, or any of them.
16(3) Parliamentary law prescribing residence requirements within a State or Union Territory.
16(4) Provision for reservation of appointments or posts in favor of any backward class of citizens not adequately represented in the services under the State.
16(4A) Reservation in matters of promotion with consequential seniority for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (77th & 85th Amendments).
16(4B) Carry-forward of unfilled vacancies without exceeding the 50% ceiling on aggregate vacancies of that year (81st Amendment).
16(6) Reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) up to 10% in public appointments (103rd Amendment).

LEGAL ANALYSIS:
Article 16 governs equal opportunity in public service. In Indra Sawhney (1992), the 9-Judge Bench held that Article 16(4) is an emphatic restatement of substantive equality under Article 16(1), not an exception. Key constitutional limits include: (a) 50% vertical reservation ceiling; (b) exclusion of the 'creamy layer' from OBC reservations; (c) backwardness must be social and educational, not purely economic; and (d) administrative efficiency under Article 335 must be preserved.

title: Article 17: Abolition of Untouchability
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: Abolition of Untouchability, Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955, SC/ST Prevention of Atrocities Act 1989, absolute fundamental right, horizontal enforcement against private individuals
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Absolute Prohibition of Untouchability and Direct Horizontal Rights Enforcement.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
'Untouchability' is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden. The enforcement of any disability arising out of 'Untouchability' shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law.

LEGAL ANALYSIS:
Article 17 is one of the rare self-executing Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution that operates horizontally against private citizens, not merely vertically against the State (People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India, 1982). The Constitution does not define 'untouchability'; the Mysore High Court in Devarajiah v. Padmanna (1958) clarified that the word refers to the social disability historically imposed on certain classes of people by reason of their birth in specific castes, rather than literal physical touch. Parliament enacted the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 pursuant to powers under Article 35(a)(ii) to give teeth to Article 17's mandate.

title: Article 18: Abolition of Titles
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: Abolition of Titles, National Awards, Bharat Ratna, Padma Vibhushan, aristocratic distinctions, republican democracy
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Abolition of Feudal and Aristocratic Distinctions in a Republican Democracy.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
18(1) No title, not being a military or academic distinction, shall be conferred by the State.
18(2) No citizen of India shall accept any title from any foreign State.
18(3) No person who is not a citizen of India shall, while holding any office of profit or trust under the State, accept without the consent of the President any title from any foreign State.
18(4) No person holding any office of profit or trust under the State shall, without the consent of the President, accept any present, emolument, or office of any kind from or under any foreign State.

LEGAL ANALYSIS:
In Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996), a Constitution Bench upheld the validity of National Awards (Bharat Ratna, Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, Padma Shri), holding that they do not constitute prohibited 'titles' within the meaning of Article 18. The court observed that Article 18 seeks to prevent the creation of a titled aristocracy and hereditary privileges antithetical to republican equality, but does not preclude recognition of noble deeds, merit, or public service. However, the court strictly mandated that recipients must not use these honors as prefixes or suffixes to their names.

title: Article 20: Protection in Respect of Conviction for Offences
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
secondary_articles: Article 21, Article 359, Code of Criminal Procedure
legal_topics: Ex post facto law, double jeopardy, protection against self-incrimination, non-suspendable right, narco-analysis, polygraph
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Fundamental Safeguards in Criminal Jurisprudence (Non-Suspendable under Emergency).

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
20(1) No person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act charged as an offence, nor be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence.
20(2) No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once (Double Jeopardy).
20(3) No person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself (Self-Incrimination).

LEGAL ANALYSIS:
Following the 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978), Article 20 cannot be suspended even during a National Emergency proclaimed under Article 352. Clause (1) prohibits retrospective criminalization and retrospective enhancement of penalties (Kedar Nath v. State of West Bengal), though it does not prohibit retrospective reduction of penalty (Rattan Lal v. State of Punjab). Clause (2) incorporates the doctrine of autrefois convict—prohibiting repeated prosecution and punishment before a court of law for the same identical offence (Maqbool Hussain v. State of Bombay). Clause (3) grants the right to silence and immunity from testimonial compulsion. In Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010), the Supreme Court ruled that involuntary administration of narco-analysis, polygraph tests, and brain-mapping violates Article 20(3) as well as the right to privacy under Article 21.

title: Article 21: Protection of Life and Personal Liberty
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: Right to Life, Personal Liberty, Procedure established by law, Substantive due process, Golden Triangle, Right to Privacy, Dignity, Livelihood, Speedy Trial, Medical Care
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Sacrosanct Heart of Fundamental Rights, Human Dignity, and Due Process of Law.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.

LEGAL ANALYSIS AND EXPANSIVE JURISPRUDENCE:
Article 21 protects every person (citizens and non-citizens alike) against arbitrary deprivation of life or personal liberty. Initially given a narrow, positivist reading in A.K. Gopalan (1950), Article 21 underwent a constitutional revolution in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978). The Supreme Court read 'procedure established by law' as requiring that any law depriving personal liberty must not be arbitrary, fanciful, or oppressive, but must be 'just, fair, and reasonable', effectively importing American substantive due process into Indian constitutionalism. Through the Golden Triangle doctrine (interconnection between Articles 14, 19, and 21), the court held that any statutory restriction under Article 21 must also withstand the equality and non-arbitrariness tests of Article 14 and the reasonableness tests of Article 19. Through decades of progressive judicial interpretation, 'life' has been held to mean far more than mere animal existence (Francis Coralie), encompassing:
• Right to human dignity (Francis Coralie Mullin, 1981)
• Right to livelihood and shelter (Olga Tellis, 1985)
• Right to privacy as an intrinsic fundamental right (K.S. Puttaswamy, 2017)
• Right to speedy trial and legal aid (Hussainara Khatoon, Khatri)
• Right against torture and custodial violence (D.K. Basu, Sunil Batra)
• Right to clean environment and pollution-free water/air (M.C. Mehta)
• Right to emergency medical care (Parmanand Katara)
• Right to die with dignity and passive euthanasia (Common Cause, Aruna Shanbaug)
• Right to bodily autonomy and sexual orientation (Navtej Johar, Joseph Shine).

title: Article 21A: Right to Free and Compulsory Education
court: Parliament of India (86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002)
bench: Enacted by Parliament of India
legal_topics: Right to education, fundamental right, children aged 6 to 14 years, RTE Act 2009, affirmative admission quotas
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Fundamental Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Elementary Education.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine.

LEGAL ANALYSIS:
Inserted by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002, Article 21A transformed the non-justiciable Directive Principle of State Policy under Article 45 into an enforceable Fundamental Right under Part III. This amendment was inspired by the landmark judgments in Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992) and Unni Krishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993), wherein the Supreme Court held that the right to education is implicit in and flows directly from the right to life with dignity under Article 21. To operationalize Article 21A, Parliament enacted the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act), mandating a 25% quota in private unaided schools for children belonging to disadvantaged and weaker sections, which was upheld by the Supreme Court in Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2012).

title: Article 22: Protection Against Arrest and Detention in Certain Cases
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: Punitive detention, preventive detention, right to be informed of grounds of arrest, right to consult legal practitioner, production before magistrate within 24 hours, Advisory Board
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Procedural Safeguards in Punitive Arrest and Constitutional Limits on Preventive Detention.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
22(1) Right to be informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for arrest, and right to consult, and to be defended by, a legal practitioner of one's choice.
22(2) Every person arrested and detained in custody shall be produced before the nearest magistrate within a period of twenty-four hours of such arrest (excluding journey time), and no detention beyond said period without magistrate's authority.
22(3) Clauses (1) and (2) do not apply to enemy aliens or persons arrested under preventive detention laws.
22(4)-(7) Safeguards governing preventive detention: detention beyond three months requires opinion of an Advisory Board comprising High Court judges; detaining authority must communicate grounds of detention and afford earliest opportunity to make a representation.

LEGAL ANALYSIS:
Article 22 provides procedural guarantees against unlawful police incarceration. In D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997), the Supreme Court derived mandatory custodial arrest guidelines directly from Articles 21 and 22(1)-(2). Preventive detention is strictly construed by courts, and any unexplained delay in deciding a detenu's representation vitiates the detention order as unconstitutional.

title: Article 23: Prohibition of Traffic in Human Beings and Forced Labour
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: Traffic in human beings, begar, forced labour, minimum wages, horizontal fundamental right, bonded labour
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Prohibition of Human Trafficking, Begar, and Extraction of Forced Labour.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
23(1) Traffic in human beings and begar and other similar forms of forced labour are prohibited and any contravention of this provision shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law.
23(2) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from imposing compulsory service for public purposes, and in imposing such service the State shall not make any discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste or class or any of them.

LEGAL ANALYSIS:
Article 23 is an absolute fundamental right enforceable against private parties as well as the State. In People's Union for Democratic Rights (PUDR) v. Union of India (Asiad Workers Case, 1982), Justice Bhagwati held that 'forced labour' is not restricted to physical compulsion or legal duress. Where a person provides physical or mental labour for remuneration less than the statutory minimum wage, the economic distress and deprivation force him to surrender his labour, which directly constitutes 'forced labour' violating Article 23.

title: Article 24: Prohibition of Employment of Children in Factories, etc.
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: Child labour, hazardous employment, factories, mines, Child Labour Prohibition Act, rehabilitation of child workers
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Absolute Prohibition on Employment of Children below Fourteen in Hazardous Occupations.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
No child below the age of fourteen years shall be employed to work in any factory or mine or engaged in any other hazardous employment.

LEGAL ANALYSIS:
Article 24 establishes an absolute, non-derogable constitutional command for the protection of children under 14 years of age. In M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu (Sivakasi Child Labour Case, 1996), the Supreme Court directed the abolition of child labour in match and fireworks factories, mandating the creation of the Child Labour Rehabilitation-cum-Welfare Fund where offending employers must pay compensation per child worker, harmonizing Article 24 with the right to education under Article 21A.

title: Article 25: Freedom of Conscience and Free Profession, Practice and Propagation of Religion
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: Freedom of religion, conscience, profession, practice, propagation, public order, morality, health, essential religious practices doctrine, social reform
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Freedom of Religion Subject to Public Order, Morality, Health, and Fundamental Rights.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
25(1) Subject to public order, morality and health and to the other provisions of this Part, all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion.
25(2) Nothing in this article shall affect the operation of any existing law or prevent the State from making any law:
(a) regulating or restricting any economic, financial, political or other secular activity associated with religious practice;
(b) providing for social welfare and reform or the throwing open of Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus.

LEGAL ANALYSIS AND ESSENTIAL RELIGIOUS PRACTICES DOCTRINE:
Article 25 protects individual religious freedom, available to citizens and non-citizens. Crucially, the right under Article 25(1) is expressly made subject to (a) public order, morality, and health; and (b) 'the other provisions of this Part'—meaning it is subordinate to Articles 14 and 21 (Indian Young Lawyers Assn - Sabarimala, 2018). Under the 'Essential Religious Practices' doctrine originated in the Shirur Mutt Case (1954), constitutional protection extends only to tenets and practices that are essential and integral to the religion, as determined objectively by the court from foundational scriptures, rather than secular or superstitious accretions.

title: Article 26: Freedom to Manage Religious Affairs
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: Religious denominations, institutional religious freedom, management of affairs in religion, movable and immovable property, Shirur Mutt test
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Collective Freedom of Religious Denominations to Manage Institutional Affairs.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
Subject to public order, morality and health, every religious denomination or any section thereof shall have the right:
(a) to establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes;
(b) to manage its own affairs in matters of religion;
(c) to own and acquire movable and immovable property; and
(d) to administer such property in accordance with law.

LEGAL ANALYSIS:
While Article 25 protects individual religious conscience, Article 26 protects collective institutional autonomy of religious denominations. To claim the status of a 'religious denomination' under the Shirur Mutt test, a group must satisfy three conditions: (1) collection of individuals with a common system of beliefs; (2) common organization; and (3) designated by a distinctive name. Unlike Article 25, Article 26 is NOT expressly made subject to other provisions of Part III, but is strictly subject to public order, morality, and health. While administration of property can be regulated by state law (clause d), matters of religion remain autonomous (clause b).

title: Article 29: Protection of Interests of Minorities
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: Cultural and educational rights, distinct language, script or culture, non-discrimination in state-aided educational institutions
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Protection of Distinct Culture, Language, and Non-Discrimination in Education.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
29(1) Any section of the citizens residing in the territory of India or any part thereof having a distinct language, script or culture of its own shall have the right to conserve the same.
29(2) No citizen shall be denied admission into any educational institution maintained by the State or receiving aid out of State funds on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language or any of them.

LEGAL ANALYSIS:
Article 29(1) confers a right on 'any section of citizens' (which can include linguistic minorities or majorities) to conserve their language, script, or culture. Article 29(2) is an individual right of every citizen against discrimination in State or State-aided educational institutions. In State of Bombay v. Bombay Education Society (1954), the Supreme Court ruled that an order prohibiting admission of students whose mother tongue was not English into English-medium schools violated Article 29(2).

title: Article 30: Right of Minorities to Establish and Administer Educational Institutions
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: Minority educational institutions, religious minorities, linguistic minorities, administrative autonomy, state aid, TMA Pai, PA Inamdar
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Fundamental Charter of Educational Autonomy for Religious and Linguistic Minorities.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
30(1) All minorities, whether based on religion or language, shall have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.
30(1A) Mandatory compensation in case of compulsory acquisition of minority institutional property to ensure right is not abrogated (44th Amendment).
30(2) The State shall not, in granting aid to educational institutions, discriminate against any educational institution on the ground that it is under the management of a minority, whether based on religion or language.

LEGAL ANALYSIS:
Article 30(1) grants religious and linguistic minorities the fundamental right to establish and administer educational institutions. In T.M.A. Pai Foundation (2002) and P.A. Inamdar (2005), an 11-Judge and 7-Judge Bench clarified: (1) Minority status is determined State-wise, not nationally; (2) The right to administer is not a right to maladminister; the State can enforce regulatory standards of academic excellence, national security, and employee welfare; (3) Unaided minority institutions enjoy total autonomy over admissions and fee structure, subject to prohibition of capitation fees and transparent merit-based selection; and (4) State aid cannot be used to extinguish minority character.

title: Article 32: Remedies for Enforcement of Fundamental Rights (Constitutional Writs)
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: Constitutional Remedies, Writs, Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, Certiorari, Public Interest Litigation (PIL), Locus Standi, Basic Structure
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: The 'Heart and Soul of the Constitution' and Bulwark of Fundamental Rights.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
32(1) The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed.
32(2) The Supreme Court shall have power to issue directions or orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, whichever may be appropriate, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by this Part.
32(3) Parliamentary power to empower other courts.
32(4) The right guaranteed by this article shall not be suspended except as otherwise provided for by this Constitution.

LEGAL ANALYSIS AND WRIT JURISDICTION:
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described Article 32 as the single most important article without which the Constitution would be a nullity. Unlike ordinary appeal jurisdiction, the right to approach the Supreme Court under Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right, making the Supreme Court the 'guarantor and protector of fundamental rights' (Romesh Thappar). The Supreme Court exercises plenary writ powers:
• Habeas Corpus: To release persons illegally detained;
• Mandamus: To command public officials or bodies to perform mandatory legal duties;
• Certiorari & Prohibition: To quash or restrain orders of inferior tribunals acting without jurisdiction or violating natural justice;
• Quo Warranto: To challenge unlawful usurpation of substantive public offices.
In Bandhua Mukti Morcha and S.P. Gupta, the court liberalized the rule of locus standi, giving birth to Public Interest Litigation (PIL) to enable disadvantaged citizens to access justice. In L. Chandra Kumar (1997), Article 32 was declared an unalterable facet of the Basic Structure.

title: Article 141: Law Declared by Supreme Court to be Binding on All Courts
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: Doctrine of Precedent, Stare Decisis, Ratio Decidendi, Obiter Dicta, Prospective Overruling, Binding nature of Supreme Court judgments
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Constitutional Inscription of Stare Decisis and Judicial Precedent.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
The law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within the territory of India.

LEGAL ANALYSIS AND DOCTRINAL PRINCIPLES:
Article 141 establishes the constitutional doctrine of binding precedent across the Indian judicial hierarchy. Key constitutional rules include:
1. Scope of 'Law Declared': What binds under Article 141 is the ratio decidendi—the underlying legal principle upon which the controversy is decided. Obiter dicta (incidental remarks) of the Supreme Court carry enormous persuasive weight, but are strictly not binding precedents.
2. 'All Courts' Excludes the Supreme Court Itself: In Bengal Immunity Co. Ltd. v. State of Bihar (1955), the Supreme Court ruled that it is not bound by its own previous decisions and may depart from or overrule earlier rulings when convinced they are erroneous or harmful to public interest.
3. Doctrine of Prospective Overruling: Established in I.C. Golaknath (1967), the Supreme Court possesses the jurisdiction to declare that an overruling judgment will operate purely prospectively, preserving the validity of past transactions while governing future legal actions.

title: Article 142: Enforcement of Decrees, Orders, and Plenary Power for Complete Justice
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: Plenary power, complete justice, inherent jurisdiction, judicial lawmaking, Vishaka guidelines, Bhopal gas tragedy, Ayodhya dispute
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Plenary Constitutional Power of the Supreme Court to Do Complete Justice.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
142(1) The Supreme Court in the exercise of its jurisdiction may pass such decree or make such order as is necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it, and any decree so passed or order so made shall be enforceable throughout the territory of India in such manner as may be prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament.
142(2) Power to secure attendance of persons, discovery of documents, or punishment for contempt.

LEGAL ANALYSIS AND LIMITS OF PLENARY POWER:
Article 142 confers extraordinary, curative powers on the Supreme Court to ensure that procedural technicalities or legislative vacuums do not prevent justice from being done. In Union Carbide Corporation v. Union of India (1991), the court held that its power under Article 142 is not bounded by statutory law, provided it does not contravene express constitutional prohibitions. In Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997), the court invoked Article 142 read with Article 32 to formulate binding workplace sexual harassment guidelines in the absence of enacted legislation. In Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India (1998), the court clarified the limits: Article 142 is a corrective power that cannot be used to subvert express statutory provisions or punish for contempt by suspending an advocate's statutory license.

title: Article 226: Power of High Courts to Issue Certain Writs
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: High Court writ jurisdiction, Fundamental Rights, Any other purpose, Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Certiorari, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, Alternative remedy, Territorial jurisdiction
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Plenary Writ Jurisdiction of High Courts for Fundamental Rights and Legal Rights.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
226(1) Notwithstanding anything in article 32, every High Court shall have power, throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction, to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases, any Government, directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose.
226(2) Territorial jurisdiction based on cause of action arising wholly or in part within the territory.

LEGAL ANALYSIS:
The writ jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226 is significantly broader in scope than the Supreme Court's Article 32 jurisdiction. While Article 32 can be invoked ONLY for the enforcement of Part III Fundamental Rights, Article 226 can be invoked for fundamental rights AND 'for any other purpose'—which includes enforcement of non-fundamental legal rights, statutory duties, and constitutional principles. However, while Article 32 is itself a guaranteed fundamental right, remedy under Article 226 is discretionary. High Courts typically decline to exercise writ jurisdiction where an effective and adequate alternative statutory remedy exists, except where fundamental rights are violated, natural justice is breached, or proceedings are completely without jurisdiction (Whirlpool Corporation v. Registrar of Trade Marks).

title: Article 300A: Persons Not to be Deprived of Property Save by Authority of Law
court: Parliament of India (44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978)
bench: Enacted by Parliament of India
legal_topics: Right to property, constitutional right, human right, eminent domain, authority of law, just compensation
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Constitutional Right Against Arbitrary Deprivation of Property.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.

LEGAL ANALYSIS:
By the 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978), the Right to Property was deleted from the Fundamental Rights chapter (repealing Articles 19(1)(f) and 31) and re-inserted as Article 300A under Part XII as a constitutional right. Though no longer a Part III fundamental right (and hence cannot be enforced directly via Article 32 without alleging another fundamental right breach), the Supreme Court in K.T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka (2011) and Vidya Devi v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2020) held that the right to property under Article 300A is a valuable constitutional right and a recognized human right. The State cannot dispossess a citizen of their property without (a) valid statutory authority; (b) a legitimate public purpose; and (c) fair and just compensation.

title: Article 352: Proclamation of Emergency
bench: Constituent Assembly / Parliament of India
legal_topics: National emergency, war, external aggression, armed rebellion, cabinet written advice, parliamentary approval, non-suspension of Articles 20 and 21
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Constitutional Framework and Strict Safeguards for Proclamation of National Emergency.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
352(1) If the President is satisfied that a grave emergency exists whereby the security of India or of any part of the territory thereof is threatened, whether by war or external aggression or armed rebellion, he may, by Proclamation, make a declaration to that effect.
352(2) Proclamation may be varied or revoked by a subsequent Proclamation.
352(3) President shall not issue a Proclamation unless the decision of the Union Cabinet (Prime Minister and other Ministers of Cabinet rank) has been communicated to him in writing.
352(4) Must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within one month by special majority (majority of total membership and not less than 2/3 of members present and voting).

LEGAL ANALYSIS:
Substantially revised by the 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) to eliminate abuses witnessed during the 1975 internal emergency: (1) The vague ground 'internal disturbance' was replaced with 'armed rebellion'; (2) Written recommendation from the entire Union Cabinet was made mandatory; (3) Parliamentary approval window was reduced from 2 months to 1 month with special majority; and (4) Articles 20 and 21 were rendered permanently non-suspendable during emergencies under Article 359.

title: Article 356: Provisions in Case of Failure of Constitutional Machinery in States (President's Rule)
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: President's Rule, State emergency, breakdown of constitutional machinery, Governor's report, federalism, basic structure, judicial review, floor test
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Judicial Review over Imposition of President's Rule and Protection of Federalism.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
356(1) If the President, on receipt of report from the Governor of a State or otherwise, is satisfied that a situation has arisen in which the government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution, the President may by Proclamation:
(a) assume to himself all or any of the functions of the Government of the State and all or any of the powers vested in or exercisable by the Governor;
(b) declare that the powers of the Legislature of the State shall be exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament.

LEGAL ANALYSIS:
Historically misused to dismiss democratically elected opposition State governments, Article 356 was subjected to strict constitutional discipline in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994). A 9-Judge Constitution Bench held that: (1) Federalism is part of the Basic Structure; (2) The President's satisfaction under Article 356 is subject to judicial review to examine if it is based on malafide, extraneous, or irrelevant grounds; (3) The State Legislative Assembly cannot be dissolved until both Houses of Parliament approve the Proclamation; and (4) The floor of the Assembly is the sole constitutional forum to test a ministry's majority, not the subjective opinion of the Governor.

title: Article 368: Power of Parliament to Amend the Constitution and Procedure Therefor
bench: Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee (Dr. B.R. Ambedkar)
legal_topics: Constitutional Amendment, Constituent Power, Basic Structure Doctrine, Judicial Review, Special Majority, Federal Ratification
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Constituent Amending Power of Parliament Bound by the Basic Structure Doctrine.

CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISION:
368(1) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may in exercise of its constituent power amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision of this Constitution in accordance with the procedure laid down in this article.
368(2) Bill must be passed in each House by a majority of total membership and a majority of not less than two-thirds of members present and voting; amendments affecting federal provisions require ratification by legislatures of not less than half the States.
368(4)-(5) Clauses inserted by 42nd Amendment seeking to exclude judicial review (struck down in Minerva Mills).

LEGAL ANALYSIS AND THE BASIC STRUCTURE BATTLE:
Article 368 contains the constituent power to amend the Constitution. The legal scope of this power represents the greatest constitutional struggle in Indian legal history:
1. Shankari Prasad (1951) & Sajjan Singh (1965): Held amending power was unlimited and could amend Fundamental Rights.
2. Golaknath (1967): 11-Judge Bench held Parliament had no power to abridge Fundamental Rights under Article 368.
3. Kesavananda Bharati (1973): 13-Judge Bench overruled Golaknath, holding that while Parliament can amend any provision including Part III, it cannot alter, damage, or destroy the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution.
4. Minerva Mills (1980): The Supreme Court struck down Clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 which claimed unlimited amending power, affirming that a limited amending power is itself a basic feature of the Constitution.

title: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
bench: 6-Judge Constitution Bench (Kania CJ, Fazal Ali, Patanjali Sastri, Mahajan, Mukherjea, Das)
legal_topics: Preventive detention, procedure established by law, formalist interpretation, mutual exclusivity of fundamental rights
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Early formalist doctrine holding that Fundamental Rights are mutually exclusive 'silos' and 'procedure established by law' means any enacted statutory procedure.

FACTS: Communist leader A.K. Gopalan was detained under Section 3(1) of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950. He challenged the detention petitioning under Article 32, asserting that detention without trial violated his personal liberty under Article 21 and freedoms under Article 19(1)(d).

ISSUE: Whether the Preventive Detention Act violated Articles 19 and 21, and whether 'procedure established by law' in Article 21 implies the American doctrine of substantive 'due process of law'.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 19(1)(d), Article 21, Article 22, Preventive Detention Act 1950.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The majority held that Articles 19 and 21 are mutually exclusive compartments. Article 19 applies only to free citizens, whereas Article 21 applies when personal liberty is taken away entirely. The court rejected the incorporation of American substantive 'due process', holding that 'procedure established by law' refers strictly to state-made enacted statutory law. Justice Fazal Ali dissented, anticipating the modern view that procedure must be fair and reasonable.

FINAL HOLDING: Preventive Detention Act upheld (save Section 14). Strict literalist interpretation adopted (later overruled in R.C. Cooper and Maneka Gandhi).

title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
bench: 7-Judge Constitution Bench (Beg CJ, Chandrachud, Bhagwati, Krishna Iyer, Untwalia, Murtaza Fazal Ali, Kailasam)
legal_topics: Right to travel abroad, substantive due process, procedure established by law, golden triangle, post-decisional hearing, natural justice
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Established substantive due process in India; ruled that 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 must be just, fair, and reasonable, and established the Golden Triangle of Articles 14, 19, and 21.

FACTS: The Regional Passport Office, New Delhi impounded Maneka Gandhi's passport under Section 10(3)(c) of the Passports Act, 1967 'in public interest' without furnishing reasons or providing a pre-decisional hearing.

ISSUE: Whether impounding a passport without giving reasons or opportunity of hearing violates fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(a)/(g), and 21.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 14, Article 19(1)(a)/(d), Article 21, Passports Act 1967 Section 10(3)(c).

RATIO DECIDENDI: Overruling Gopalan, the 7-Judge Bench held that Part III rights do not exist in watertight silos but form an interconnected 'Golden Triangle' (Articles 14, 19, and 21). Any law depriving personal liberty must satisfy not only Article 21, but also the non-arbitrariness test of Article 14 and reasonableness tests of Article 19. The phrase 'procedure established by law' cannot be an arbitrary or oppressive statutory procedure; it must be 'just, fair, and reasonable', thereby introducing substantive due process into Indian constitutional law.

FINAL HOLDING: Right to travel abroad is an integral component of personal liberty under Article 21. Natural justice (audi alteram partem) is mandatory; post-decisional hearing accepted in this specific case.

title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India
bench: 9-Judge Constitution Bench (Khehar CJ, Chelameswar, Bobde, Chandrachud, Nariman, Kaul, Nazeer, Sapre, Agrawal)
legal_topics: Right to Privacy, informational privacy, bodily autonomy, spatial privacy, proportionality standard, overruling MP Sharma and Kharak Singh
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Unanimously held that the Right to Privacy is a fundamental right emanating intrinsically from Article 21, life, dignity, and Part III liberties.

FACTS: Retired High Court Judge K.S. Puttaswamy challenged the constitutional validity of the Union Government's Aadhaar biometric identification scheme, arguing that mandatory collection of fingerprints and iris scans violated the fundamental right to privacy.

ISSUE: Whether privacy is a fundamental right guaranteed under Part III of the Constitution, and whether earlier larger bench rulings in M.P. Sharma (1954, 8 Judges) and Kharak Singh (1963, 6 Judges) correctly held that privacy is not a fundamental right.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 14, Article 19, Article 21, Part III.

RATIO DECIDENDI: All 9 judges unanimously declared privacy to be a fundamental right intrinsic to life, personal liberty, and human dignity under Article 21, permeating Part III. Privacy encompasses informational privacy, bodily privacy, and decisional autonomy. The court expressly overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent they denied privacy as a fundamental right, and explicitly overruled the majority in ADM Jabalpur (1976). Any state intrusion on privacy must satisfy the strict three-fold proportionality test: (1) Legality (backed by valid law); (2) Legitimate state aim; and (3) Proportionality (least restrictive means).

FINAL HOLDING: Right to Privacy affirmed as a fundamental right under Article 21.

title: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
bench: 13-Judge Constitution Bench (Sikri CJ, Shelat, Hegde, Grover, Ray, Reddy, Palekar, Khanna, Mathew, Beg, Dwivedi, Mukherjea, Chandrachud)
legal_topics: Basic Structure Doctrine, constituent power, constitutional amendments, limits on amending power, judicial review
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Formulated the Basic Structure Doctrine; held that Parliament's constituent power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 does not extend to altering or destroying its basic features.

FACTS: His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati, head of Edneer Mutt, challenged the Kerala Land Reforms Act and the 24th, 25th, and 29th Constitutional Amendments, which sought to bypass judicial review of property acquisition.

ISSUE: What is the extent of Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368, and whether Parliament can abrogate Fundamental Rights.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 13, Article 31C, Article 368, 24th, 25th, 29th Amendments.

RATIO DECIDENDI: By a historic 7-6 majority, the 13-Judge Bench overruled Golaknath and held that Parliament has wide constituent powers under Article 368 to amend any provision of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights. However, this power is not unlimited; Parliament cannot alter the 'Basic Structure' or essential constitutional framework. Basic features include supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secularism, separation of powers, federalism, judicial review, and the rule of law.

FINAL HOLDING: 24th Amendment upheld; second part of Article 31C (barring judicial review) struck down as unconstitutional. Basic Structure doctrine established as the supreme judicial safeguard.

title: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (Chandrachud CJ, Gupta, Untwalia, Kailasam, Bhagwati)
legal_topics: Basic structure, limited amending power, judicial review, harmony between fundamental rights and directive principles
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Held that limited amending power under Article 368 and judicial review are themselves basic features; Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles must exist in harmonious balance.

FACTS: Minerva Mills, a textile undertaking nationalized under the Sick Textile Undertakings Act 1974, challenged Sections 4 and 55 of the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.

ISSUE: Whether Parliament can expand its amending power under Article 368 into an absolute, unlimited power immune from judicial review.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 368(4), Article 368(5), Article 31C, Article 14, Article 19.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The Supreme Court struck down Clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368. Chief Justice Y.V. Chandrachud observed that a limited amending power is one of the basic features of our Constitution and therefore the limitations on that power cannot be destroyed. Parliament cannot convert a limited power into an unlimited one. The court also struck down the unamended portion of Article 31C that gave absolute primacy to all DPSPs over Articles 14 and 19, observing that Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are like two wheels of a chariot.

FINAL HOLDING: Sections 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment declared unconstitutional. Basic Structure doctrine vigorously reaffirmed.

title: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (Ray CJ, Palekar, Chandrachud, Bhagwati, Krishna Iyer)
legal_topics: New doctrine of equality, anti-arbitrariness, rule of law, administrative discretion, civil services
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Formulated the new dynamic doctrine of equality, establishing that equality is antithetical to arbitrariness under Article 14.

FACTS: E.P. Royappa, Chief Secretary of Tamil Nadu, was transferred to newly created non-cadre posts (Officer on Special Duty). He challenged the transfer alleging malafide action by Chief Minister M. Karunanidhi and violation of Articles 14 and 16.

ISSUE: Whether arbitrary executive transfer violates Articles 14 and 16, and what constitutes the conceptual scope of equality.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 14, Article 16.

RATIO DECIDENDI: Justice P.N. Bhagwati propounded the transformative 'anti-arbitrariness' doctrine of equality: 'Equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects and dimensions and it cannot be 'cribbed, cabined and confined' within traditional and doctrinaire limits. From a positivistic point of view, equality is antithetical to arbitrariness. In fact equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies; one belongs to the rule of law in a republic while the other, to the whim and caprice of an absolute monarch.' Where an act is arbitrary, it implicitly breaches equality.

FINAL HOLDING: Transfer was upheld on facts, but the groundbreaking anti-arbitrariness doctrine became the bedrock of modern Article 14 jurisprudence.

title: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (Mandal Case)
bench: 9-Judge Constitution Bench (Kania CJ, Venkatachaliah, Ahmadi, Shetty, Verma, Sawant, Ramaswamy, Thommen, Sahai)
legal_topics: OBC reservation, Mandal Commission, creamy layer exclusion, 50% ceiling limit, promotions, backwardness criteria
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Upheld 27% reservation for Other Backward Classes (OBCs) subject to creamy layer exclusion and strict 50% reservation ceiling limit.

FACTS: The V.P. Singh government implemented the Mandal Commission recommendations, reserving 27% of public service posts for Socially and Educationally Backward Classes (OBCs). Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao later added a 10% economic quota for poorer upper castes.

ISSUE: Constitutional validity of 27% OBC reservation under Article 16(4), definition of backward classes, creamy layer exclusion, and 50% limit.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 16(1), Article 16(4), Article 15(4), Article 340, Article 335.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The 9-Judge Bench held that: (1) Article 16(4) is an emphatic restatement of equality, not an exception to Article 16(1); (2) Caste can be an acceptable starting metric to identify backward classes, provided social and educational backwardness is established; (3) The 'creamy layer' (socially and economically advanced members) must be excluded from OBC reservations; (4) Total reservations under Article 16(4) must not exceed 50% except in extraordinary regional circumstances; (5) Article 16(4) applies only to initial appointments, not promotions; and (6) The 10% economic criteria quota without backwardness was invalid.

FINAL HOLDING: 27% OBC reservation upheld subject to creamy layer exclusion and 50% cap.

title: Shayara Bano v. Union of India
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (Khehar CJ, Kurian Joseph, Nariman, U.U. Lalit, Abdul Nazeer)
legal_topics: Triple Talaq, Talaq-e-biddat, manifest arbitrariness, Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937, gender justice, essential religious practice
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Declared instantaneous Triple Talaq (Talaq-e-biddat) unconstitutional under the doctrine of 'Manifest Arbitrariness' under Article 14.

FACTS: Shayara Bano was divorced by her husband through instantaneous triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat). She filed a writ petition under Article 32 challenging the constitutional validity of triple talaq, polygamy, and nikah halala.

ISSUE: Whether instantaneous Triple Talaq is protected under Article 25 as an essential religious practice, and whether it violates Articles 14, 15, and 21.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 14, Article 15, Article 21, Article 25, Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937 Section 2.

RATIO DECIDENDI: By a 3-2 majority, the Constitution Bench set aside talaq-e-biddat. Justice Nariman and Justice Lalit held that triple talaq is recognized by the 1937 Shariat Act, making it 'law' within the meaning of Article 13. They established the doctrine of 'Manifest Arbitrariness' under Article 14: statutory provisions or customs that are capricious, irrational, or devoid of determining principle violate Article 14. Because triple talaq allows a husband to arbitrarily terminate marriage without reconciliation, it is manifestly arbitrary. Justice Kurian Joseph concurred on the ground that what is bad in theology (Quran) cannot be good in law.

FINAL HOLDING: Practice of Talaq-e-biddat declared unconstitutional, void, and illegal.

title: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (Misra CJ, Khanwilkar, Chandrachud, Nariman, Malhotra)
legal_topics: Decriminalization of Section 377 IPC, LGBTQ+ rights, constitutional morality, bodily autonomy, sexual orientation, non-discrimination
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Decriminalized consensual homosexual acts between adults; held that sexual orientation is an intrinsic component of Article 21 privacy and Article 14 equality.

FACTS: Members of the LGBTQ+ community, including dancer Navtej Singh Johar, challenged the constitutionality of Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code, which criminalized 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature'.

ISSUE: Whether Section 377 IPC violates fundamental rights of LGBTQ+ individuals under Articles 14, 15, 19, and 21, and whether Suresh Koushal (2014) was wrongly decided.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 14, Article 15(1), Article 19(1)(a), Article 21, Section 377 IPC.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The 5-Judge Constitution Bench unanimously struck down Section 377 IPC insofar as it criminalizes consensual sexual conduct between adults of the same sex. Chief Justice Dipak Misra and Justice Chandrachud propounded the doctrine of 'Constitutional Morality' over majoritarian social morality. Sexual orientation is a core natural attribute of identity, personal liberty, and human dignity protected by Article 21. Discrimination based on sexual orientation is sex discrimination under Article 15(1). Suresh Koushal was expressly overruled.

FINAL HOLDING: Section 377 declared unconstitutional regarding consensual adult relationships. Historical apology tendered to the LGBTQ+ community.

title: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
bench: 2-Judge Bench (Chelameswar, Nariman)
legal_topics: Freedom of speech online, Section 66A Information Technology Act, vagueness, chilling effect, discussion vs advocacy vs incitement
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act for overbreadth, vagueness, and chilling free speech online under Article 19(1)(a).

FACTS: Two young women were arrested under Section 66A of the IT Act for posting and liking comments on Facebook questioning the total shutdown of Mumbai following the death of a political leader. Law student Shreya Singhal challenged Section 66A via PIL.

ISSUE: Whether Section 66A of the IT Act violates freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) and does not qualify as a reasonable restriction under Article 19(2).

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 19(1)(a), Article 19(2), Section 66A IT Act 2000.

RATIO DECIDENDI: Justice Rohinton Nariman drew a critical constitutional distinction between three concepts: (1) Discussion, (2) Advocacy, and (3) Incitement. Mere discussion or advocacy of an unpopular cause cannot be criminalized under Article 19(2); speech can only be restricted when it reaches the threshold of incitement to violence or public disorder. Section 66A was unconstitutionally vague and overbroad because terms like 'annoyance', 'inconvenience', and 'grossly offensive' lacked objective statutory definition, creating a severe chilling effect on speech.

FINAL HOLDING: Section 66A of the IT Act struck down in its entirety as unconstitutional and void.

title: Siddharam Satlingappa Mhetre v. State of Maharashtra
bench: 2-Judge Bench (Dalveer Bhandari, K.S. Radhakrishnan)
legal_topics: Anticipatory bail, personal liberty, Section 438 CrPC, arrest safeguards, presumption of innocence
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Ruled that anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC is a direct derivative of personal liberty under Article 21 and cannot be arbitrarily curtailed by rigid time limits.

FACTS: Appellant Siddharam Mhetre was implicated in a politically motivated FIR under Section 302 IPC. The High Court rejected his anticipatory bail application.

ISSUE: Scope and ambit of anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC, whether courts can impose artificial time limits on pre-arrest bail, and its relationship with Article 21.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 21, Section 438 Code of Criminal Procedure 1973.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The Supreme Court held that the right to anticipatory bail is intrinsically linked to the sanctity of personal liberty guaranteed under Article 21. Arbitrary arrests cause irreparable humiliation and reputational damage. The court held that Section 438 must be interpreted expansively to protect citizens against unjustified harassment. Imposing artificial expiry dates or restricting bail until the filing of the chargesheet contradicts the legislative intent of Section 438.

FINAL HOLDING: Anticipatory bail should ordinarily continue until the conclusion of trial unless exceptional circumstances warrant cancellation.

title: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
bench: 2-Judge Bench (Kuldip Singh, A.S. Anand)
legal_topics: Custodial violence, torture, arrest guidelines, memo of arrest, right to medical examination, right to inform next of kin
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Formulated 11 mandatory guidelines governing arrest and detention to eradicate custodial torture and deaths under Article 21.

FACTS: Executive Chairman of Legal Aid Services, West Bengal addressed a letter regarding frequent custodial deaths and police violence, which the Supreme Court treated as a PIL.

ISSUE: Whether custodial torture, assault, and death in police lockups violate fundamental rights under Article 21 and Article 22, and what procedural safeguards must be mandated.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 21, Article 22, Code of Criminal Procedure.

RATIO DECIDENDI: Custodial violence, torture, and lock-up deaths strike at the very soul of the rule of law and human dignity protected under Article 21. Any form of torture or cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment of detainees falls foul of Article 21, whether during investigation or interrogation. The court exercised judicial lawmaking to lay down 11 mandatory directions (such as identifying arresting officers, preparing an arrest memo witnessed by an independent person, informing family within 8-12 hours, and conducting medical examinations every 48 hours).

FINAL HOLDING: 11 D.K. Basu arrest guidelines made mandatory across India; custodial violence made subject to strict departmental and criminal contempt liability.

title: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
bench: 3-Judge Bench (Verma CJ, Sujata Manohar, Kirpal)
legal_topics: Workplace sexual harassment, Vishaka guidelines, CEDAW convention, judicial lawmaking, gender equality, safe work environment
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Formulated the historic 'Vishaka Guidelines' against workplace sexual harassment, deriving enforceable norms from Articles 14, 19, 21, and international treaties under Article 142.

FACTS: Bhanwari Devi, a social worker in Rajasthan campaigning against child marriage, was brutally gang-raped. The trial court acquitted the accused. Social action groups filed a PIL for women's workplace safety.

ISSUE: In the absence of domestic legislation, can the Supreme Court formulate binding norms under Articles 32 and 142 to prevent workplace sexual harassment?

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 14, Article 15, Article 19(1)(g), Article 21, Article 142, CEDAW.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The Supreme Court held that sexual harassment in the workplace violates gender equality (Articles 14 & 15), the right to carry on trade/profession (Article 19(1)(g)), and the right to life with dignity (Article 21). In the absence of domestic legislation, international conventions like CEDAW must be read into fundamental rights under Article 142 to fill legislative vacuums.

FINAL HOLDING: Mandatory Vishaka Guidelines issued requiring Internal Complaints Committees (ICC) in all workplaces (later codified into the POSH Act, 2013).

title: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
bench: 9-Judge Constitution Bench (Ratnavel Pandian, Ahmadi, Kuldip Singh, Verma, Sawant, Ramaswamy, Agarwal, Reddy, Sen)
legal_topics: President's rule, dissolution of State assemblies, federalism, secularism as basic structure, judicial review of presidential proclamation, floor test
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Subordinated the exercise of President's Rule under Article 356 to strict judicial review; affirmed Federalism and Secularism as unalterable Basic Features.

FACTS: Karnataka Chief Minister S.R. Bommai's government was dismissed under Article 356 following alleged defecting legislators, without being allowed a floor test. Several State governments were similarly dismissed.

ISSUE: Scope of judicial review over Presidential Proclamation under Article 356, power to dissolve State assemblies, and status of secularism and federalism.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 356, Article 74(2), Article 355, Basic Structure.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The 9-Judge Bench laid down seminal constitutional rules: (1) Federalism and Secularism are essential parts of the Basic Structure; (2) The President's power under Article 356 is conditional, and the proclamation is subject to judicial review; (3) The Legislative Assembly cannot be dissolved until both Houses of Parliament approve the Proclamation; (4) If the proclamation is struck down as malafide or unconstitutional, the court has the power to resurrect the dismissed ministry and restore the dissolved Assembly; (5) The floor of the House is the only valid forum to test majority, not Raj Bhavan.

FINAL HOLDING: Proclamations in Karnataka and Meghalaya held unconstitutional; federal discipline enforced on Article 356.

title: Secretary, State of Karnataka v. Umadevi (3)
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (Sabharwal CJ, Arun Kumar, G.P. Mathur, C.K. Thakker, P.K. Balasubramanyan)
legal_topics: Public employment, contractual appointments, regularisation, rule of law, back-door entry, Article 16 open competition
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Ruled that temporary, contractual, and ad-hoc employees have no fundamental right to regularization in public employment without open competition under Article 16.

FACTS: Temporary and daily-wage workers appointed in various Karnataka departments sought regularization of service based on long years of service, citing Article 14.

ISSUE: Can courts direct regularization of contractual, daily-wage, or ad-hoc public workers when appointments bypassed constitutional recruitment procedures under Articles 14 and 16?

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 14, Article 16, Article 309.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The Constitution Bench ruled that public employment must conform to Articles 14 and 16, guaranteeing open competition, equal opportunity, and merit-based recruitment. Regularizing employees who obtained 'back-door entry' without fair selection deprives qualified citizens of their constitutional right to compete for public posts. Courts cannot issue mandamus directing regularization of illegal appointments, though irregular employees who served 10 years or more without court orders could be considered as a one-time measure.

FINAL HOLDING: Commercial or compassionate regularization barred; adherence to constitutional recruitment mandates affirmed.

title: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (Pavement Dwellers Case)
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (Chandrachud CJ, Murtaza Fazal Ali, Tulzapurkar, Reddy, Varadarajan)
legal_topics: Right to livelihood, pavement dwellers, eviction without notice, natural justice, estoppel against fundamental rights
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Right to Life under Article 21 includes the Right to Livelihood; no person can be evicted from shelter without procedural fairness and natural justice.

FACTS: In 1981, Bombay Municipal Corporation and Maharashtra State undertook forcible eviction and demolition of thousands of pavement and slum dwellings without prior notice or alternative rehabilitation.

ISSUE: Whether the right to life guaranteed by Article 21 includes the right to livelihood, and whether municipal authorities can evict pavement dwellers without prior notice.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 21, Article 14, Article 19(1)(e), Bombay Municipal Corporation Act 1888 Section 314.

RATIO DECIDENDI: Chief Justice Y.V. Chandrachud delivered the unanimous ruling: 'An important facet of the right to life is the right to livelihood. If the right to livelihood is not treated as a part of the constitutional right to life, the easiest way of depriving a person of his life would be to deprive him of his means of livelihood.' To deprive a person of their livelihood is to strip their life of its meaningful content. Even though public footpaths are meant for pedestrian transit, municipal authorities exercising power of eviction under Section 314 must adhere to procedural natural justice and provide reasonable notice and hearing before demolition.

FINAL HOLDING: Right to livelihood declared an integral part of Article 21. Evictions must be humane, giving adequate opportunity and alternate transit sites where feasible.

title: Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi
bench: 2-Judge Bench (Bhagwati, Murtaza Fazal Ali)
legal_topics: Right to live with human dignity, prisoners' rights, COFEPOSA detenu, family visits, right to legal counsel
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Right to Life means the Right to Live with Human Dignity, not mere animal existence or physical survival.

FACTS: British national Francis Coralie Mullin was detained in Tihar Central Jail under the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act (COFEPOSA). She was restricted from interviewing her lawyer and seeing her young daughter without bureaucratic permissions.

ISSUE: Whether arbitrary restrictions on a prisoner's right to meet family and legal counsel violate fundamental rights under Article 21.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 21, Article 14, COFEPOSA Detention Conditions.

RATIO DECIDENDI: Justice P.N. Bhagwati articulated the foundational dignity jurisprudence: 'We think that the right to life includes the right to live with human dignity and all that goes along with it, namely, the bare necessaries of life such as adequate nutrition, clothing and shelter and facilities for reading, writing and expressing oneself in diverse forms.' The right to life under Article 21 cannot be restricted to mere animal existence. A prisoner or preventive detenu retains all constitutional fundamental rights except those legitimately curtailed by detention. Denying a detenu access to counsel and family is an unreasonable deprivation of dignity.

FINAL HOLDING: Detenu has a fundamental right under Article 21 to meet legal counsel and family members without humiliating obstacles.

title: Hussainara Khatoon (I to VI) v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar
bench: 3-Judge Bench (Bhagwati, Koshal, Sen)
legal_topics: Right to speedy trial, undertrial prisoners, free legal aid, bail reforms, systemic criminal injustice
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Established the Right to Speedy Trial and Free Legal Aid as essential fundamental rights under Article 21.

FACTS: An investigative series of articles in the Indian Express exposed thousands of undertrial prisoners languishing in Bihar jails for decades, awaiting trial for periods far exceeding the maximum statutory sentence for their alleged offences. Advocate Pushpa Kapila Hingorani filed a habeas corpus PIL.

ISSUE: Whether prolonged detention of undertrials without trial violates Article 21, and whether the right to speedy trial and legal aid are fundamental rights.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 21, Article 39A, Section 167 CrPC.

RATIO DECIDENDI: Justice P.N. Bhagwati held that 'speedy trial' is an integral and essential part of the fundamental right to life and personal liberty enshrined in Article 21. No procedure which does not ensure a reasonably quick trial can be regarded as 'just, fair, and reasonable' under the Maneka Gandhi test. The state cannot plead administrative or financial inability to deny this right. The court also held that free legal aid to impoverished accused facing imprisonment is an implicit constitutional command under Article 21 and Article 39A.

FINAL HOLDING: Immediate release of over 40,000 undertrials ordered. Right to speedy trial affirmed as a constitutional guarantee.

title: Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration
bench: 3-Judge Bench (Krishna Iyer, Pathak, Reddy)
legal_topics: Prisoners' rights, bar fetters, solitary confinement, custodial torture, epistolary jurisdiction, judicial monitoring
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Enforced constitutional rights within prison walls; held that convicts are not denuded of fundamental rights and prohibited solitary confinement.

FACTS: Sunil Batra, a death-row prisoner in Tihar Jail, sent a handwritten letter on scrap paper to Supreme Court Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer reporting that a jail warden had brutally assaulted another prisoner (Prem Chand) to extort money. The court treated the letter as a habeas corpus petition.

ISSUE: Can courts intervene under Article 32 to protect prisoners against custodial torture, and whether prisoners lose their fundamental rights upon incarceration.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 14, Article 19, Article 21, Article 32, Prisons Act 1894 Sections 30, 46, 56.

RATIO DECIDENDI: Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer laid down that conviction for a crime does not reduce a human being to a non-person. Prisoners retain all fundamental rights under Part III, subject only to those deprivations necessitated by the fact of imprisonment. Solitary confinement, imposition of iron fetters, and physical torture without judicial authority violate Articles 14, 19, and 21. The court affirmed 'epistolary jurisdiction'—allowing letters from prisoners to activate the court's writ power.

FINAL HOLDING: Inhuman prison practices and arbitrary solitary confinement declared unconstitutional; district judges empowered to inspect prisons regularly.

title: Selvi v. State of Karnataka
bench: 3-Judge Bench (Balakrishnan CJ, Raveendran, Dalveer Bhandari)
legal_topics: Narco-analysis, polygraph lie-detector, BEAP brain-mapping, self-incrimination, mental privacy, bodily autonomy, forced testimony
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Involuntary administration of narco-analysis, polygraph, and brain-mapping violates the protection against self-incrimination under Article 20(3) and mental privacy under Article 21.

FACTS: Petitioners challenged the involuntary use of neuro-scientific investigative techniques (Narco-analysis using sodium pentothal, Polygraph test, and Brain Electrical Activation Profile / BEAP) on accused persons without their consent.

ISSUE: Whether forced administration of neuro-scientific investigative techniques violates Article 20(3) (protection against self-incrimination) and Article 21 (right to privacy and bodily integrity).

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 20(3), Article 21, Section 161(2) CrPC, Indian Evidence Act Section 27.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The Supreme Court held that the compulsory administration of narco-analysis, polygraph, and brain-mapping violates the right against self-incrimination under Article 20(3). Forcible intrusion into an individual's subconscious mental processes deprives them of the choice between speech and silence. Furthermore, subjecting an individual to such physical and mental intrusion without consent violates bodily integrity and the 'mental privacy' facet of personal liberty under Article 21. The court permitted such tests ONLY when voluntarily undergone, but held that test results themselves cannot be admitted as substantive evidence.

FINAL HOLDING: Involuntary narco-analysis, polygraph, and brain-mapping declared unconstitutional and inadmissible in evidence.

title: Common Cause v. Union of India
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (Misra CJ, Sikri, Khanwilkar, Chandrachud, Ashok Bhushan)
legal_topics: Passive euthanasia, advance medical directive, living will, right to die with dignity, vegetative state, medical autonomy
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Recognized the fundamental right to die with dignity as part of Article 21 and legalized passive euthanasia and advance medical directives (Living Wills).

FACTS: NGO Common Cause filed a writ petition seeking recognition of the right to die with dignity and the execution of living wills for terminally ill patients in permanent vegetative states.

ISSUE: Whether the right to life with dignity under Article 21 includes the right to die with dignity, and whether passive euthanasia and advance medical directives are legally permissible.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 21, Medical Council of India Regulations.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The 5-Judge Constitution Bench unanimously affirmed that the right to life under Article 21 encompasses the right to live with dignity up to the point of death, including a dignified dying process. Prolonging terminal agony through artificial life-support systems against a patient's informed autonomy violates Article 21. The court recognized the distinction between active euthanasia (which remains an offence) and passive euthanasia (withholding or withdrawing life support), holding passive euthanasia permissible under strict medical safeguards. It recognized the constitutional validity of 'Advance Medical Directives' (Living Wills).

FINAL HOLDING: Passive euthanasia and Living Wills legalized; detailed procedural guidelines laid down to protect terminally ill patients.

title: People's Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL) v. Union of India (Telephone Tapping Case)
bench: 2-Judge Bench (Kuldip Singh, Saghir Ahmad)
legal_topics: Telephone tapping, right to privacy, surveillance, freedom of speech, procedural safeguards, Review Committee
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Held that telephone tapping infringes the Right to Privacy under Article 21 and Freedom of Speech under Article 19(1)(a) unless strictly justified by public emergency.

FACTS: PUCL challenged the rampant, uncontrolled interception and tapping of telephone conversations of political leaders and citizens by government intelligence agencies under Section 5(2) of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885.

ISSUE: Whether telephone tapping violates the right to privacy under Article 21 and freedom of expression under Article 19(1)(a), and whether statutory safeguards are mandatory.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 19(1)(a), Article 19(2), Article 21, Section 5(2) Indian Telegraph Act 1885.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The Supreme Court held that telephonic conversations are an intimate part of modern private life. Intercepting or tapping telephone calls constitutes a direct invasion of an individual's privacy under Article 21 and impermissibly curtails freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). Telephone tapping under Section 5(2) of the Telegraph Act can ONLY be sanctioned upon the occurrence of a 'public emergency' or in the interest of 'public safety'. In the absence of statutory procedural safeguards, the court formulated mandatory guidelines requiring authorizations to be issued only by the Home Secretary, valid for max 2 months, and reviewed by a Cabinet Review Committee.

FINAL HOLDING: Strict procedural safeguards mandated for telephone surveillance; arbitrary state tapping held unconstitutional.

title: Joseph Shine v. Union of India
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (Misra CJ, Khanwilkar, Nariman, Chandrachud, Malhotra)
legal_topics: Decriminalization of adultery, gender equality, stereotyping of women as property, manifest arbitrariness, marital privacy
content:
