LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Decriminalized adultery by striking down Section 497 IPC as a sexist, patriarchal relic violating Articles 14, 15, and 21.

FACTS: Petitioner Joseph Shine challenged the constitutional validity of Section 497 of the Indian Penal Code, which penalized a man for having sexual intercourse with the wife of another man without the husband's consent, but exempted the woman from criminal liability and gave no remedy to a wife whose husband committed adultery.

ISSUE: Whether Section 497 IPC violates Articles 14, 15, and 21 by treating women as chattel and property of their husbands.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 14, Article 15(1), Article 21, Section 497 Indian Penal Code, Section 198(2) CrPC.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The 5-Judge Constitution Bench unanimously struck down Section 497 IPC and Section 198(2) CrPC. The court held that Section 497 is manifestly arbitrary under Article 14 because it treats a married woman as the chattel/property of her husband—exempting adultery if the husband consents. It violates Article 15(1) by perpetuating entrenched gender stereotypes regarding female subservience. Furthermore, criminalizing private sexual autonomy in marriage without public harm violates personal dignity and bodily autonomy under Article 21. Adultery may remain a civil ground for divorce, but cannot be a criminal offence.

FINAL HOLDING: Section 497 IPC struck down as unconstitutional and void.

title: Kharak Singh v. State of UP
bench: 6-Judge Constitution Bench (Sinha CJ, Imam, Subba Rao, Shah, Raghubar Dayal, Rajagopala Ayyangar)
legal_topics: History-sheeting, secret picketing, domiciliary visits, early privacy jurisprudence, Justice Subba Rao dissent
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Held midnight domiciliary police visits unconstitutional under Article 21; seminal dissent of Justice Subba Rao that Right to Privacy is an integral part of personal liberty.

FACTS: Kharak Singh was acquitted of dacoity due to lack of evidence, but UP Police opened a history-sheet against him under Chapter XX of the UP Police Regulations, subjecting him to secret surveillance, periodic domiciliary visits at night, and verification of movements.

ISSUE: Whether police surveillance and midnight domiciliary visits violate Article 19(1)(d) (freedom of movement) and Article 21 (personal liberty).

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 19(1)(d), Article 21, Regulation 236 UP Police Regulations.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The majority struck down Regulation 236(b) authorizing midnight domiciliary visits, holding that knocking on a citizen's door at night disrupts rest and psychological peace, violating personal liberty under Article 21. However, the majority held that secret picketing did not violate movement under Article 19(1)(d) and stated that privacy was not a guaranteed constitutional right. In a visionary dissent, Justice K. Subba Rao held that the right to privacy is an integral ingredient of personal liberty under Article 21, arguing that all surveillance without authority of law violates the Constitution.

FINAL HOLDING: Domiciliary visits struck down; Subba Rao's dissent was later vindicated and adopted as unanimous law in Puttaswamy (2017).

title: M.P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra
bench: 8-Judge Constitution Bench (Mahajan CJ, Mukherjee, Das, Bose, Hasan, Bhagwati, Jagannadhadas, Venkatarama Ayyar)
legal_topics: Search and seizure, self-incrimination under Article 20(3), private papers, absence of express Fourth Amendment equivalent
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Early ruling that search and seizure under valid warrants does not violate Article 20(3); noted the absence of an express privacy provision in the Constitution (later overruled in Puttaswamy).

FACTS: In an investigation into Dalmia group companies for misappropriation and fraud, the District Magistrate issued search warrants under Section 96 CrPC, seizing large volumes of private books and documents.

ISSUE: Whether search and seizure of private papers from an accused violates Article 20(3) (protection against self-incrimination) and the right to privacy.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 20(3), Article 19(1)(f), Section 96 Code of Criminal Procedure 1898.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The 8-Judge Bench held that search and seizure under a warrant is an overriding state power for investigation of crimes and does not equate to testimonial compulsion under Article 20(3). The court remarked that the framers of the Indian Constitution did not include a provision analogous to the Fourth Amendment of the US Constitution protecting against unreasonable searches. This literal observation was used for decades by the State to argue that privacy was not a fundamental right.

FINAL HOLDING: Search and seizure upheld; observations denying privacy were formally overruled by the 9-Judge Bench in Puttaswamy (2017).

title: ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (Habeas Corpus Case)
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (Ray CJ, Beg, Chandrachud, Bhagwati, H.R. Khanna)
legal_topics: Internal emergency, presidential order under Article 359, suspension of Article 21, locus standi for habeas corpus, Justice H.R. Khanna dissent
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Infamous majority ruling holding that during Emergency under Article 359, no citizen had locus standi to file habeas corpus against illegal detention; historic dissent of Justice H.R. Khanna.

FACTS: Following the declaration of Internal Emergency in June 1975, the President issued an order under Article 359(1) suspending the right to move any court for enforcement of Articles 14, 21, and 22. Thousands of political leaders were detained under MISA without trial.

ISSUE: Whether in view of the Presidential Order under Article 359, a writ petition for habeas corpus under Article 226 was maintainable to challenge illegal, malafide detentions.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 21, Article 359(1), Article 226, MISA Section 16A.

RATIO DECIDENDI: By a 4-1 majority, the court held that during Emergency, Article 21 was the sole repository of the right to life and liberty; upon its suspension under Article 359, no person had standing to seek judicial relief against deprivation of liberty, even if the detention was unlawful or malafide. Justice H.R. Khanna delivered his immortal dissent: 'Life and personal liberty are not the bounty of the State or the creation of the Constitution. Even in the absence of Article 21, the State has no power to deprive a person of his life or liberty without authority of law. A dissent in a court of last resort is an appeal to the brooding spirit of the law, to the intelligence of a future day.'

FINAL HOLDING: Majority judgment declared bad in law by Parliament via 44th Amendment (making Article 21 non-suspendable) and officially overruled in Puttaswamy (2017).

title: I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab
bench: 11-Judge Constitution Bench (Subba Rao CJ, Wanchoo, Hidayatullah, Shah, Sikri, Bachawat, Ramaswami, Shelat, Bhargava, Mitter, Vaidialingam)
legal_topics: Constituent power, amendment as 'law' under Article 13(2), transcendental fundamental rights, prospective overruling
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: 11-Judge Bench held that Fundamental Rights are transcendental and Parliament had no power under Article 368 to abridge or take away Part III rights; established Doctrine of Prospective Overruling.

FACTS: Henry and William Golaknath challenged the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, and the 17th Constitutional Amendment which placed the Act into the Ninth Schedule, immunizing it from judicial review under Part III.

ISSUE: Whether an amendment to the Constitution made under Article 368 is a 'law' within the meaning of Article 13(2), and whether Parliament can take away Fundamental Rights.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 13(2), Article 368, 17th Constitutional Amendment.

RATIO DECIDENDI: By a 6-5 majority, Chief Justice K. Subba Rao held that: (1) Article 368 contains merely the procedure for amendment, not plenary constituent power; (2) An amendment to the Constitution is a 'law' under Article 13(2), and any amendment taking away Fundamental Rights is void; (3) Fundamental Rights are given a transcendental position; and (4) Invoking American jurisprudence, the court introduced the Doctrine of Prospective Overruling—holding that past amendments (1st, 4th, 17th) remained valid, but Parliament had no future power to amend Part III.

FINAL HOLDING: Parliament barred from abridging Fundamental Rights (later overruled in Kesavananda Bharati, leading to the Basic Structure doctrine).

title: Waman Rao v. Union of India
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (Chandrachud CJ, Bhagwati, Krishna Iyer, Tulzapurkar, Sen)
legal_topics: Cut-off date for basic structure review, Ninth Schedule immunity, prospective application post-April 24, 1973
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Established April 24, 1973 (date of Kesavananda Bharati) as the constitutional watershed cut-off date for testing Ninth Schedule laws against the Basic Structure Doctrine.

FACTS: The Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961 was placed in the Ninth Schedule by the 40th Constitutional Amendment. Petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of Articles 31A, 31B, and 31C as violating the basic structure.

ISSUE: Whether amendments placing enactments in the Ninth Schedule after the Kesavananda Bharati verdict are subject to basic structure review.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 31A, Article 31B, Article 31C, Article 368, Ninth Schedule.

RATIO DECIDENDI: Chief Justice Y.V. Chandrachud reconciled Ninth Schedule immunity with the Basic Structure doctrine by establishing a definitive temporal boundary: All constitutional amendments and enactments included in the Ninth Schedule PRIOR to April 24, 1973 (the date Kesavananda was delivered) are constitutionally protected and immune from challenge. However, all amendments and laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule ON OR AFTER April 24, 1973 are open to constitutional scrutiny and can be struck down if they violate the basic structure of the Constitution.

FINAL HOLDING: Cut-off date established; prospective applicability of basic structure review to Ninth Schedule affirmed.

title: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (Ninth Schedule Case)
bench: 9-Judge Constitution Bench (Sabharwal CJ, Lakshmanan, Mathur, Pasayat, Balasubramanyan, Thakker, Sinha, Kapadia, Raveendran)
secondary_articles: Article 31B, Article 14, Article 19, Article 21, Ninth Schedule
legal_topics: Ninth Schedule judicial review, blanket immunity rejected, 'rights test' vs 'essence of rights test', basic structure touchstone
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Unanimously held that laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule post-April 24, 1973 enjoy no blanket immunity and are subject to judicial review against Part III and the Basic Structure.

FACTS: Following conflicting interpretations between Waman Rao and Minerva Mills regarding the extent of judicial scrutiny over laws placed in the Ninth Schedule under Article 31B, the matter was referred to a 9-Judge Constitution Bench.

ISSUE: Can Parliament immunize laws from judicial review by placing them in the Ninth Schedule, and what is the test for constitutional invalidity of Ninth Schedule laws?

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 31B, Article 14, Article 19, Article 21, Article 368, Ninth Schedule.

RATIO DECIDENDI: Chief Justice Y.K. Sabharwal delivered the unanimous 9-judge ruling: There is no blanket immunity for any law inserted into the Ninth Schedule on or after April 24, 1973. While Article 31B protects ordinary statutory violations, if a Ninth Schedule law abrogates fundamental rights that form part of the Basic Structure (Articles 14, 19, and 21), that law is unconstitutional. The court formulated the 'Rights Test' and 'Essence of Rights Test': Any law destroying the golden triangle or rule of law violates the basic structure.

FINAL HOLDING: Ninth Schedule laws post-April 24, 1973 are subject to full judicial review; parliamentary immunity cannot override the Basic Structure.

title: R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (Bank Nationalization Case)
bench: 11-Judge Constitution Bench (Shah, Sikri, Shelat, Grover, Hegde, Ray, Reddy, Palekar, Dua, Vaidialingam, Hidayatullah CJ)
legal_topics: Bank nationalization, mutual exclusivity rejected, effect test of legislation, right to compensation, direct and inevitable effect
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Overruled Gopalan's mutual exclusivity doctrine; held that the validity of state action must be tested by its 'effect' on fundamental rights rather than legislative form or subject matter.

FACTS: R.C. Cooper, a shareholder and director of Central Bank of India, challenged the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1969, which nationalized 14 major commercial banks and provided illusory compensation while barring them from general banking.

ISSUE: Whether the Act violated Articles 14, 19(1)(f), and 31(2), and whether fundamental rights are mutually exclusive or interconnected.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 14, Article 19(1)(f), Article 31(2), Banking Companies Act 1969.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The 11-Judge Bench (10-1) discarded the formalist Gopalan doctrine that fundamental rights are mutually exclusive water-tight compartments. Justice J.C. Shah established the 'Effect Test' (Direct and Inevitable Effect): The constitutional validity of state action is determined not by the object or legislative subject matter, but by its direct operation and inevitable effect on fundamental rights. A law affecting property under Article 31 must also satisfy the test of reasonableness under Article 19(1)(f) and non-arbitrariness under Article 14. Compensation must be an equivalent in money representing genuine value.

FINAL HOLDING: Bank Nationalization Act struck down for discriminatory compensation and unreasonable barriers (paving the way for Maneka Gandhi's Golden Triangle).

title: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan
bench: 7-Judge Constitution Bench (Kania CJ, Fazal Ali, Sastri, Mahajan, Mukherjea, Das, Bose)
legal_topics: Communal G.O., reservations in education, Fundamental Rights supremacy over Directive Principles, genesis of First Constitutional Amendment
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Held that Fundamental Rights are supreme and cannot be overridden by Directive Principles of State Policy; led directly to the First Constitutional Amendment enacting Article 15(4).

FACTS: The Madras Government issued a 'Communal G.O.' allocating fixed quotas in medical and engineering colleges based strictly on religion, caste, and race. Brahmin candidates denied admission challenged the order under Article 29(2).

ISSUE: Can the State justify caste-based educational quotas under Directive Principle Article 46 when it violates the fundamental right against discrimination under Article 29(2)?

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 15(1), Article 29(2), Article 46.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The 7-Judge Bench held that the Communal G.O. violated Article 29(2) because admission was denied based solely on religion and caste. The court declared that the Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) cannot override or abridge Fundamental Rights (Part III); Directive Principles must conform to and run subsidiary to Fundamental Rights. In response to this ruling, Parliament enacted the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, introducing Article 15(4) to permit special affirmative provisions for backward classes and SC/STs.

FINAL HOLDING: Communal G.O. struck down; foundational milestone for educational reservation jurisprudence.

title: Shankari Prasad v. Union of India
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (Kania CJ, Sastri, Mukherjea, Das, Chandrasekhara Aiyar)
legal_topics: First Amendment validity, constituent power vs ordinary legislative power, power to amend Fundamental Rights
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: First major constitutional bench ruling on amending power; held that constituent power under Article 368 is distinct from ordinary legislative power and can amend Fundamental Rights.

FACTS: Landlords challenged the validity of the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, which inserted Articles 31A and 31B (and the Ninth Schedule) to insulate agrarian land reform laws from fundamental rights challenge.

ISSUE: Whether Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 is limited by Article 13(2) prohibiting laws abridging Fundamental Rights.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 13(2), Article 368, 1st Amendment Act 1951.

RATIO DECIDENDI: Chief Justice Patanjali Sastri held that there is a clear demarcation between ordinary legislative power exercised by Parliament and constituent power exercised under Article 368. The word 'law' in Article 13(2) refers to rules and regulations made in the exercise of ordinary legislative power, and does not include an amendment to the Constitution made in exercise of constituent power. Therefore, Parliament can amend any provision of the Constitution, including Part III Fundamental Rights.

FINAL HOLDING: First Constitutional Amendment upheld as valid.

title: Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (Gajendragadkar CJ, Wanchoo, Hidayatullah, Shah, Mudholkar)
legal_topics: Seventeenth Amendment, seeds of Basic Structure, Justice Mudholkar and Justice Hidayatullah dissents
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Upheld the 17th Amendment; visionary dissents of Justice Hidayatullah and Justice J.R. Mudholkar planted the conceptual seeds of the Basic Structure Doctrine.

FACTS: Landowners challenged the 17th Amendment Act, 1964, which added several state land acquisition acts to the Ninth Schedule.

ISSUE: Whether the 17th Amendment fell within Article 368 and whether the unanimous ruling in Shankari Prasad should be reconsidered.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 13(2), Article 368, 17th Amendment.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The majority upheld the 17th Amendment reaffirming Shankari Prasad. However, Justice Hidayatullah expressed grave doubts on whether fundamental rights could be the plaything of a legislative majority. Crucially, Justice J.R. Mudholkar questioned whether Parliament could alter the 'basic features' of the Constitution, drawing from the concept of unamendable provisions in the Pakistani Constitution, noting that every Constitution has certain foundational features that cannot be rewritten.

FINAL HOLDING: 17th Amendment upheld, but seminal judicial doubts led directly to Golaknath (1967) and Kesavananda (1973).

title: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras
bench: 6-Judge Constitution Bench (Kania CJ, Fazal Ali, Sastri, Mahajan, Mukherjea, Das)
secondary_articles: Article 32, Section 9(1-A) Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act 1949
legal_topics: Freedom of speech and expression, freedom of the press, circulation of journals, public safety vs public order
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Established that Freedom of the Press is an implicit fundamental right under Article 19(1)(a) and struck down pre-censorship and ban on circulation.

FACTS: The Government of Madras banned the entry and circulation of Romesh Thappar's weekly journal 'Cross Roads' under the Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act, 1949 'for the purpose of securing public safety and maintaining public order'.

ISSUE: Whether freedom of circulation is part of Article 19(1)(a) and whether 'public safety' fell within the permitted restrictions under the unamended Article 19(2).

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 19(1)(a), Article 19(2), Article 32.

RATIO DECIDENDI: Justice Patanjali Sastri held that freedom of speech and expression includes the freedom of propagation of ideas, and that freedom is ensured by the freedom of circulation: 'Without circulation, the publication would be of little value.' The court made a strict distinction between maintaining public order and undermining the security of the State. At that time, Article 19(2) did not contain 'public order' (which was subsequently inserted by the First Amendment). Banning the circulation of a journal violated Article 19(1)(a).

FINAL HOLDING: Ban on circulation quashed; press freedom declared fundamental.

title: Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (Sikri CJ, Ray, Reddy, Palekar, Beg)
legal_topics: Freedom of the press, newsprint allocation policy, page-limit restriction, direct and inevitable effect, commercial liberty
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Struck down government newsprint restrictions that capped newspaper page numbers, reaffirming that press freedom cannot be strangulated through administrative rationing.

FACTS: The Union Government formulated the Newsprint Control Order and Newsprint Allocation Policy for 1972-73, imposing a rigid 10-page ceiling on major daily newspapers and prohibiting inter-changeability of newsprint among editions.

ISSUE: Whether newsprint page ceilings and quota controls violate freedom of the press under Article 19(1)(a) and equality under Article 14.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 19(1)(a), Article 19(2), Article 14.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The Supreme Court applied the R.C. Cooper 'direct and inevitable effect' test. While the government may legitimately regulate the import and distribution of scarce commodities like newsprint, it cannot use quota regulations as a subterranean mechanism to dictate the volume, size, and circulation of newspapers. Capping pages directly reduced editorial space and advertisement revenue, curtailing circulation and crippling freedom of expression under Article 19(1)(a).

FINAL HOLDING: 10-page limit and restrictive allocation policies struck down as unconstitutional.

title: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India
bench: 3-Judge Bench (Ramana, Reddy, Gavai)
secondary_articles: Article 21, Section 144 CrPC, Telecom Suspension Rules 2017
legal_topics: Internet shutdown in Jammu & Kashmir, freedom of speech and trade over internet, proportionality test, publication of suspension orders
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Declared that freedom of speech and expression and freedom of trade/business over the internet are fundamental rights under Article 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g); indefinite internet shutdowns are illegal.

FACTS: Following the abrogation of Article 370 in August 2019, the government imposed sweeping communications blackouts, internet shutdowns, and Section 144 movement restrictions across Jammu & Kashmir. Executive Editor of Kashmir Times, Anuradha Bhasin, challenged the indefinite lockdown.

ISSUE: Whether access to the internet is protected under Article 19, whether indefinite internet suspensions are constitutionally permissible, and whether orders must be published.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 19(1)(a), Article 19(1)(g), Article 19(2), Section 144 CrPC, Telecom Suspension Rules.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The Supreme Court held that: (1) Freedom of speech and expression and the right to practice any profession or business over the medium of the internet are constitutionally protected under Article 19(1)(a) and Article 19(1)(g); (2) An indefinite suspension of internet services is impermissible and violates the doctrine of proportionality; (3) Suspension orders must satisfy the strict proportionality test (legitimate aim, suitability, necessity, least restrictive measure); (4) State must publish all suspension orders to enable judicial review; and (5) Section 144 CrPC cannot be used as a tool to suppress legitimate expression of democratic grievances.

FINAL HOLDING: Indefinite internet bans declared unconstitutional; periodic review mandated.

title: Aruna Ramchandra Shanbaug v. Union of India
bench: 2-Judge Bench (Katju, Mishra)
legal_topics: Passive euthanasia guidelines, permanent vegetative state, brain-dead patient, withdrawal of life support, parens patriae
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Laid down landmark guidelines legalizing passive euthanasia in India subject to High Court approval under parens patriae jurisdiction.

FACTS: Aruna Shanbaug, a nurse at KEM Hospital Mumbai, was brutally assaulted and suffocated with a dog chain in 1973, leaving her in a permanent vegetative state (PVS) for 37 years. Activist Pinki Virani filed a writ petition seeking directions to stop feeding and allow her to die peacefully.

ISSUE: Whether passive euthanasia (withdrawing life support/nutrition) should be permitted for a patient in a permanent vegetative state under Article 21.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 21, Section 309 IPC.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The Supreme Court clarified the distinction between active euthanasia (administering a lethal injection, which remains illegal murder) and passive euthanasia (withdrawing artificial life-sustaining mechanisms to allow nature to take its course). The court held that passive euthanasia is legally permissible under strict judicial oversight. Until Parliament enacts a statute, any decision to withdraw life support requires: (1) Approval of parents/spouse or close medical attendants; (2) Opinion of a board of 3 medical experts; and (3) Mandatory approval by a Division Bench of the High Court under Article 226.

FINAL HOLDING: Passive euthanasia recognized; on facts, permission denied because hospital staff wished to care for Aruna.

title: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (First Judges Case)
bench: 7-Judge Constitution Bench (Bhagwati, Gupta, Fazal Ali, Tulzapurkar, Desai, Pathak, Venkataramiah)
legal_topics: Judicial appointments, executive primacy, consultation vs concurrence, locus standi liberalization, Public Interest Litigation (PIL)
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Held that 'consultation' in judicial appointments does not mean 'concurrence' (granting executive primacy); revolutionized PIL by dramatically liberalizing locus standi.

FACTS: Petitions challenged the mass transfer of High Court judges and non-appointment of additional judges during the post-Emergency era.

ISSUE: Scope of 'consultation' with Chief Justice of India under Articles 124(2) and 217(1), and whether practicing lawyers have standing to challenge judicial appointments.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 124(2), Article 217(1), Article 32, Article 226.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The 7-Judge Bench delivered two monumental rulings: (1) On judicial appointments, the majority held that 'consultation' does not mean 'concurrence'. The President (Executive) is not bound by the opinion of the CJI, giving the central government ultimate primacy in judicial appointments (later overruled in the Second Judges case); (2) On access to justice, Justice P.N. Bhagwati revolutionized Indian jurisprudence by dismantling traditional strict locus standi rules. Any public-spirited individual or NGO can invoke Article 32 or 226 to seek redress for legal wrongs suffered by impoverished or oppressed classes who cannot access court.

FINAL HOLDING: Executive primacy upheld in appointments (overruled in 1993); Public Interest Litigation (PIL) permanently institutionalized.

title: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (Second Judges Case)
bench: 9-Judge Constitution Bench (Sharma CJ, Pandian, Ahmadi, Kuldip Singh, Verma, Dayal, Reddy, Ray, Sen)
legal_topics: Collegium system establishment, consultation means concurrence, CJI primacy, independence of judiciary as basic structure
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Overruled S.P. Gupta; established the Collegium System and ruled that 'consultation' means 'concurrence' of the Chief Justice of India and senior colleagues.

FACTS: SC Advocates-on-Record Association filed a writ petition seeking reconsideration of S.P. Gupta to insulate the higher judiciary from executive interference and filling vacancies.

ISSUE: Does executive primacy in judicial appointments compromise judicial independence, and should 'consultation' under Article 124(2) mean 'concurrence'?

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 124(2), Article 217(1), Basic Structure.

RATIO DECIDENDI: By a 7-2 majority, the 9-Judge Bench overruled the First Judges Case. Justice J.S. Verma held that the independence of the judiciary is an integral component of the Basic Structure. To protect this independence, the opinion of the Chief Justice of India must be given primacy in appointments and transfers of judges. 'Consultation' effectively implies concurrence. However, the CJI cannot act individually; the CJI must form an institutional consensus after consulting a collegium of the two senior-most Supreme Court judges (later expanded to four in the Third Judges Case 1998 Advisory Opinion).

FINAL HOLDING: Collegium system established; executive primacy in judicial appointments extinguished.

title: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (NJAC / Fourth Judges Case)
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (Khehar, Chelameswar, Lokur, Kurian Joseph, Goel)
legal_topics: National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC), 99th Constitutional Amendment, independence of judiciary as basic structure, collegium restored
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Struck down the 99th Constitutional Amendment and NJAC Act, holding that judicial primacy in appointments is an indispensable part of the Basic Structure.

FACTS: Parliament enacted the Constitution (Ninety-Ninth Amendment) Act, 2014, and the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) Act, replacing the Collegium system with a 6-member commission comprising the CJI, two senior SC judges, Union Law Minister, and two eminent persons.

ISSUE: Whether the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act violate the Basic Structure by eroding the independence of the judiciary and separation of powers.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 124(2), Article 124A, 124B, 124C, Article 368, 99th Amendment Act.

RATIO DECIDENDI: By a 4-1 majority, the Constitution Bench struck down both the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act as unconstitutional. The court held that judicial independence is a non-negotiable basic feature of the Constitution. Giving the Executive (Law Minister) and two 'eminent persons' a veto over judicial appointments violates the separation of powers and poses a fatal hazard to judicial independence. Judicial primacy in appointments cannot be compromised.

FINAL HOLDING: 99th Amendment struck down; Collegium system fully restored.

title: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India
bench: 7-Judge Constitution Bench (Verma CJ, Ramaswamy, Anand, Bharucha, Majmudar, Sujata Manohar, Kirpal)
legal_topics: Administrative tribunals, exclusion of High Court writ jurisdiction, judicial review as basic structure, CAT orders subject to High Court Division Bench
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Ruled that judicial review under Articles 226/227 and 32 is an unalterable Basic Feature; struck down statutory exclusion of High Court jurisdiction over tribunals.

FACTS: Section 28 of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 and Article 323A(2)(d) excluded the jurisdiction of all courts, including High Courts under Articles 226/227, over service matters decided by the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT).

ISSUE: Can Parliament or State Legislatures exclude the writ jurisdiction of High Courts and the Supreme Court by creating statutory tribunals?

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 32, Article 226, Article 227, Article 323A, Article 323B.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The 7-Judge Constitution Bench unanimously held that the power of judicial review vested in the High Courts under Articles 226/227 and the Supreme Court under Article 32 is an integral and untransferable part of the Basic Structure. Clause 2(d) of Article 323A and Clause 3(d) of Article 323B excluding High Court jurisdiction are unconstitutional. Administrative Tribunals can act as supplemental courts of first instance, but all their decisions are subject to the supervisory writ jurisdiction of a Division Bench of the High Court under Article 226/227.

FINAL HOLDING: Statutory exclusion of High Court review declared void; judicial review firmly secured as part of the Basic Structure.

title: T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka
bench: 11-Judge Constitution Bench (Kirpal CJ, Pattanaik, Rajendra Babu, Quadri, Ruma Pal, Variava, Shivraj Patil, Pasayat, Bhan, Agrawal, Lakshmanan)
legal_topics: Minority educational institutions, state-wise determination of minority, unaided private colleges, autonomy in admissions, prohibition of capitation fee
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: 11-Judge Bench held that religious and linguistic minority status is determined state-wise; established administrative and financial autonomy of unaided private educational institutions.

FACTS: Private aided and unaided professional colleges challenged sweeping state regulations controlling fee structures, seat allocations, and admission quotas in Karnataka and other states.

ISSUE: What is the unit for determining religious and linguistic minorities under Article 30, and what is the extent of government control over unaided private institutions?

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 19(1)(g), Article 26, Article 29, Article 30.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The 11-Judge Bench laid down: (1) Linguistic and religious minority status under Article 30 must be determined taking the State as the demographic unit, not the nation as a whole; (2) The right to establish and administer educational institutions is guaranteed to all citizens under Article 19(1)(g) and to minorities under Article 30; (3) Private unaided educational institutions have maximum autonomy in fee structure and admissions, provided admissions are transparent and merit-based; (4) Capitation fees and profiteering are strictly prohibited; and (5) State regulation of aided institutions can be greater to ensure academic standards.

FINAL HOLDING: Autonomy of private unaided professional colleges affirmed; minority status fixed state-wise.

title: P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra
bench: 7-Judge Constitution Bench (Lahoti CJ, Balakrishnan, Sema, S.B. Sinha, G.P. Mathur, Balasubramanyan, P.K. Balasubramanyan)
legal_topics: State quotas in private unaided colleges, reservations in unaided institutions, common entrance test, NRI quotas
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Ruled that the State cannot impose reservation quotas on private unaided professional educational institutions (led to 93rd Amendment enacting Article 15(5)).

FACTS: Private unaided professional engineering and medical colleges challenged state government orders appropriating percentage quotas for state reservations and capping fees.

ISSUE: Can the State impose affirmative action/reservations on private unaided minority and non-minority institutions without statutory or constitutional authorization?

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 19(1)(g), Article 30, Article 15.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The 7-Judge Bench unanimously held that the State cannot compel private unaided educational institutions to implement government reservation policies or surrender seats to a State quota. Imposing reservations on an unaided institution constitutes an unreasonable restriction under Article 19(6) and violates minority autonomy under Article 30. Unaided institutions are entitled to conduct admissions through a fair, transparent, and non-exploitative Common Entrance Test (CET). (Parliament subsequently enacted the 93rd Constitutional Amendment, 2005, introducing Article 15(5) to overturn this restriction).

FINAL HOLDING: State quota reservations in private unaided institutions quashed.

title: Lily Thomas v. Union of India
bench: 2-Judge Bench (Patnaik, Mukhopadhaya)
secondary_articles: Article 191, Representation of the People Act 1951 Section 8(4)
legal_topics: Criminalization of politics, disqualification of convicted legislators, unconstitutionality of Section 8(4) RPA, immediate disqualification
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Struck down Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act; held that convicted MPs and MLAs stand immediately disqualified upon conviction.

FACTS: Advocate Lily Thomas challenged Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, which allowed sitting MPs and MLAs convicted of serious crimes to retain their legislative seats if they filed an appeal within 3 months.

ISSUE: Whether Parliament had the legislative competence under Articles 102(1)(e) and 191(1)(e) to provide a special immunity shield against disqualification for sitting legislators.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 102(1)(e), Article 191(1)(e), Section 8(4) RPA 1951.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The Supreme Court held that Articles 102(1)(e) and 191(1)(e) of the Constitution govern disqualification of candidates as well as sitting members alike. The Constitution does not confer any power on Parliament to create a discriminatory dual standard shielding convicted sitting legislators from immediate disqualification while barring ordinary citizens. Section 8(4) was ultra vires the Constitution. Sitting MPs and MLAs sentenced to not less than 2 years imprisonment stand immediately disqualified from the date of conviction.

FINAL HOLDING: Section 8(4) of RPA declared unconstitutional; automatic disqualification upon conviction established.

title: Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms (ADR)
bench: 3-Judge Bench (Shah, Agrawal, Lakshmanan)
secondary_articles: Article 324, Representation of the People Act 1951
legal_topics: Voters' right to know, disclosure of candidate criminal antecedents, assets, educational qualifications, electoral transparency
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Established that voters have a Fundamental Right to Know under Article 19(1)(a) regarding criminal antecedents, assets, and qualifications of electoral candidates.

FACTS: Association for Democratic Reforms (ADR) filed a writ petition seeking directions to compel candidates contesting parliamentary and assembly elections to disclose their criminal backgrounds, financial assets, and educational qualifications.

ISSUE: Does the voter have a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(a) to know the background of candidates seeking election to public office?

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 19(1)(a), Article 324, Representation of the People Act 1951.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The Supreme Court ruled that democracy cannot survive without free and informed choice. The freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) includes the right to impart and receive information. A citizen cannot cast an intelligent and meaningful vote in a democratic election without knowing the background, criminal records, pending charges, assets/liabilities, and educational qualifications of the candidate. Under Article 324, the Election Commission has plenary powers to require mandatory disclosure affidavits.

FINAL HOLDING: Mandatory disclosure affidavits of candidate antecedents enforced for all elections.

title: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (Sabharwal CJ, Balakrishnan, S.H. Kapadia, C.K. Thakker, P.K. Balasubramanyan)
legal_topics: SC/ST reservations in promotions, backwardness, inadequacy of representation, administrative efficiency, quantifiable data
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Upheld constitutional amendments enabling SC/ST reservations in promotions, subject to the State proving backwardness, inadequacy of representation, and efficiency with quantifiable data.

FACTS: General category employees challenged the 77th, 81st, 82nd, and 85th Constitutional Amendments which inserted Articles 16(4A) and 16(4B) permitting consequential seniority in promotions for SCs/STs and carry-forward of unfilled vacancies.

ISSUE: Whether constitutional amendments enabling promotional reservations alter the Basic Structure by abrogating the 50% ceiling and merit principles.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 16(4A), Article 16(4B), Article 335, Article 368.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The Constitution Bench upheld the amendments as enabling provisions. However, the court held that the exercise of power under Article 16(4A) is subject to three mandatory constitutional conditions: The State must show in each case by quantifiable data (1) the backwardness of the class, (2) the inadequacy of representation in the specific service/cadre, and (3) that overall administrative efficiency under Article 335 is not compromised. Furthermore, promotional quotas must respect the 50% ceiling and creamy layer exclusion.

FINAL HOLDING: Amendments upheld; quantifiable data on representation and efficiency mandated before implementing promotional quotas.

title: Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (Misra CJ, Kurian Joseph, Nariman, U.U. Lalit, Ashok Bhushan)
legal_topics: Creamy layer application to SC/ST promotions, Nagaraj modification, quantifiable data on backwardness struck down
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Modified Nagaraj by holding that the State need not collect quantifiable data on backwardness for SC/STs, but affirmed that the 'Creamy Layer' principle applies to SC/ST promotions.

FACTS: The Union of India sought a referral of M. Nagaraj to a 7-Judge Bench, arguing that requiring quantifiable data on the backwardness of SCs and STs violated the Presidential Orders under Articles 341 and 342.

ISSUE: Does requiring quantifiable data on SC/ST backwardness run contrary to Indra Sawhney, and does the creamy layer exclusion apply to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in promotions?

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 16(4A), Article 341, Article 342, Article 335.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The 5-Judge Bench held that Nagaraj's requirement to collect quantifiable data on the backwardness of SCs/STs was contrary to Indra Sawhney (which held that SC/STs are inherently backward) and invalidated that specific requirement. However, the court firmly held that the 'Creamy Layer' principle is an essential facet of equality under Articles 14 and 16(1). The socially and economically advanced members of SC/STs cannot walk away with promotional benefits at the expense of genuinely impoverished members of the community.

FINAL HOLDING: No data on backwardness required for SC/ST; Creamy Layer principle holds good for SC/ST reservations in promotions.

title: Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (Sabarimala Case)
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (Misra CJ, Khanwilkar, Nariman, Chandrachud, Indu Malhotra)
legal_topics: Women entry in Sabarimala temple, biological discrimination, physiological exclusion, constitutional morality, religious denomination test
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Struck down the exclusion of women aged 10-50 from entering the Sabarimala temple as a violation of Articles 14, 15, 21, and 25; elevated Constitutional Morality over social stigma.

FACTS: Rule 3(b) of the Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship (Authorization of Entry) Rules, 1965 prohibited women aged 10 to 50 years (menstruating women) from entering the Sabarimala Ayyappa temple in Kerala.

ISSUE: Does the prohibition of women of menstruating age violate Articles 14, 15, and 21, or is it protected under Article 26 as an essential religious practice of a religious denomination?

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 14, Article 15(1), Article 21, Article 25, Article 26, Kerala Entry Rules 1965 Rule 3(b).

RATIO DECIDENDI: By a 4-1 majority, the Constitution Bench held that: (1) Ayyappa devotees do not constitute a separate religious denomination under Article 26, but are part of the larger Hindu faith; (2) Excluding women based on biological/physiological factors like menstruation is a form of untouchability and discrimination violating Articles 14, 15, and 21; (3) Freedom of religion under Article 25(1) is guaranteed equally to all persons and is expressly subject to Part III; and (4) 'Constitutional Morality' requires the eradication of misogynistic and discriminatory practices in public religious spaces. (Justice Indu Malhotra dissented on judicial review over religious beliefs).

FINAL HOLDING: Rule 3(b) struck down; women of all ages permitted to enter Sabarimala temple.

title: National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) v. Union of India
bench: 2-Judge Bench (K.S. Radhakrishnan, A.K. Sikri)
legal_topics: Transgender rights, third gender recognition, gender identity self-determination, bodily autonomy, affirmative action
content:
LANDMARK PRINCIPLE: Legally recognized transgender persons as the 'Third Gender'; affirmed self-determination of gender identity as an inalienable facet of Article 21 liberty and dignity.

FACTS: NALSA filed a writ petition highlighting systemic social exclusion, violence, and non-recognition of transgender, hijra, and kinner individuals under the binary legal framework of male/female.

ISSUE: Whether non-recognition of transgender persons as a third gender violates Articles 14, 15, 19, and 21 of the Constitution.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS: Article 14, Article 15, Article 16, Article 19(1)(a), Article 21, Yogyakarta Principles.

RATIO DECIDENDI: The Supreme Court held that gender identity is an intrinsic aspect of human personality, self-determination, and personal liberty protected under Article 21. Forcing individuals into a binary male/female classification against their self-identified gender violates their dignity. Discrimination based on 'sex' in Articles 15 and 16 includes discrimination based on gender identity. The court granted constitutional recognition to transgender persons as a 'third gender' and directed the State to treat them as socially and educationally backward classes for affirmative action and educational reservations.

FINAL HOLDING: Right of transgender persons to self-determine gender affirmed; affirmative protection and welfare measures mandated.

title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India [Ratio 01: Substantive Due Process]
bench: 7-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: Substantive due process, procedure established by law, just fair and reasonable test
content:
[Case: Maneka Gandhi v Union of India
Citation: AIR 1978 SC 597
Article: 21]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: The phrase 'procedure established by law' in Article 21 cannot be an arbitrary, oppressive, or fanciful statutory procedure. It must strictly conform to the principles of natural justice and be 'just, fair, and reasonable', effectively importing substantive due process into Indian constitutional law.

HOLDING: Any enacted procedure that deprives a person of life or personal liberty is unconstitutional under Article 21 if it lacks fairness, equity, or reasonableness.

COURT REASONING: The court reasoned that 'law' in Article 21 is not mere state-enacted legislation. A procedure established by law cannot be arbitrary, otherwise Article 21 would offer no real protection against despotic state enactments. Reasonableness is an essential element of equality and non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and therefore procedure under Article 21 must be reasonable, right, and just.

title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India [Ratio 02: Golden Triangle]
bench: 7-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: Golden triangle, mutual interdependence of fundamental rights, non-arbitrariness
content:
[Case: Maneka Gandhi v Union of India
Citation: AIR 1978 SC 597
Article: 21]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: Fundamental Rights under Part III do not operate as isolated, mutually exclusive silos; rather, Articles 14, 19, and 21 form an indivisible, interconnected trinity known as the 'Golden Triangle'.

HOLDING: A law depriving personal liberty under Article 21 must simultaneously satisfy the equality and non-arbitrariness mandates of Article 14 and the reasonableness tests under Article 19.

COURT REASONING: Justice Bhagwati rejected the Gopalan doctrine of mutually exclusive fundamental rights. The principle of reasonableness which legally as well as philosophically informs Article 14 must also permeate Article 21. Any law that is arbitrary under Article 14 is inherently unreasonable and cannot constitute valid 'procedure established by law' under Article 21.

title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India [Ratio 03: Post-Decisional Hearing]
bench: 7-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: Natural justice, audi alteram partem, post-decisional hearing, impounding passport
content:
[Case: Maneka Gandhi v Union of India
Citation: AIR 1978 SC 597
Article: 21]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: The rule of natural justice (audi alteram partem) is an essential facet of fairness and non-arbitrariness under Articles 14 and 21; where pre-decisional hearing would defeat the statutory object, a prompt post-decisional hearing satisfies natural justice.

HOLDING: While impounding a passport without giving reasons is unconstitutional, affording a fair post-decisional hearing cures the initial procedural defect.

COURT REASONING: The court observed that natural justice is not an unruly horse or a mechanical ritual. Although administrative urgency may occasionally justify dispensing with prior notice before seizing a passport to prevent flight from justice, the authority must immediately thereafter provide a full opportunity of being heard and communicate the reasons for the impoundment.

title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India [Ratio 01: Privacy as Intrinsic Right]
bench: 9-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: Fundamental right to privacy, informational privacy, bodily autonomy, decisional privacy
content:
[Case: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India
Citation: (2017) 10 SCC 1
Article: 21]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: The Right to Privacy is a fundamental and inalienable right emanating intrinsically from the guarantee of life, personal liberty, and human dignity under Article 21, and is grounded in the foundational freedoms of Part III.

HOLDING: Privacy is protected as an essential aspect of dignity, encompassing spatial privacy, bodily privacy, informational privacy, and personal decisional autonomy.

COURT REASONING: Justice D.Y. Chandrachud writing for the bench explained that privacy is the constitutional core of human dignity. It enables individuals to preserve their autonomy, control dissemination of intimate information, and protect their physical and psychological integrity against State and private encroachment.

title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India [Ratio 02: Three-Fold Proportionality Test]
bench: 9-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: Proportionality standard, legitimacy, necessity, least restrictive means, state intrusion on privacy
content:
[Case: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India
Citation: (2017) 10 SCC 1
Article: 21]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: Any State intrusion into personal privacy under Article 21 must satisfy a rigorous three-fold constitutional test of proportionality.

HOLDING: To legitimately restrict privacy, the State must prove: (1) Legality (action backed by a valid statutory law); (2) Legitimate State Aim (must serve a compelling state interest); and (3) Proportionality (rational nexus and the least restrictive measure adopted).

COURT REASONING: An infringement of privacy cannot be justified by mere executive guidelines. The law must prevent arbitrary state discretion, contain procedural safeguards against data abuse, and ensure that the extent of rights deprivation is strictly proportionate to the objective sought.

title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India [Ratio 03: Overruling MP Sharma, Kharak Singh & ADM Jabalpur]
bench: 9-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: Overruling precedent, MP Sharma, Kharak Singh, ADM Jabalpur, HR Khanna dissent vindicated
content:
[Case: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India
Citation: (2017) 10 SCC 1
Article: 21]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: The decisions in M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1963) are formally overruled to the extent they held that privacy is not a fundamental right; the majority judgment in ADM Jabalpur (1976) is declared profoundly flawed and expressly overruled.

HOLDING: Precedents denying privacy or sanctioning suspension of personal liberty during emergency are discarded from Indian constitutional jurisprudence.

COURT REASONING: The 9-Judge Bench held that the textual absence of the word 'privacy' in Part III does not negate its existence, as fundamental rights protect unenumerated core liberties. The court celebrated Justice H.R. Khanna's dissent in ADM Jabalpur, declaring that life and personal liberty pre-date the Constitution and can never be extinguished by executive decree.

title: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala [Ratio 01: Basic Structure Doctrine]
bench: 13-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: Basic structure doctrine, constituent amending power, unamendable core, supremacy of constitution
content:
[Case: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala
Citation: (1973) 4 SCC 225
Article: 368]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: Parliament's constituent power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 is broad but not unlimited; it does not include the power to alter, damage, or destroy the 'Basic Structure' or foundational identity of the Constitution.

HOLDING: The word 'amend' in Article 368 implies retaining the original constitutional identity; Parliament cannot destroy its own constitutional creator.

COURT REASONING: Chief Justice Sikri and the majority held that the Constitution is not a tabula rasa that can be dismantled by a temporary legislative majority. The constituent power to amend is distinct from the power to enact a new Constitution. Foundational features like republican democracy, secularism, separation of powers, and judicial review form the bedrock of the constitutional structure and cannot be abrogated.

title: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala [Ratio 02: Judicial Review as Basic Feature]
bench: 13-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: Judicial review, Article 31C second part struck down, exclusion of judicial scrutiny void
content:
[Case: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala
Citation: (1973) 4 SCC 225
Article: 368]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: Judicial review of legislation is an essential basic feature of the Constitution; any constitutional amendment or statute that ousts judicial review is ultra vires and void.

HOLDING: The second clause of Article 31C, which barred courts from questioning whether an enactment actually gave effect to Directive Principles, was struck down as unconstitutional.

COURT REASONING: The court ruled that Parliament cannot confer upon itself or state legislatures conclusive authority to immunize their laws from judicial examination. An ouster of judicial review destroys the balance of power and violates the Basic Structure.

title: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India [Ratio 01: Limited Amending Power as Basic Feature]
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: Limited amending power, basic structure, striking down 42nd Amendment Section 55
content:
[Case: Minerva Mills Ltd. v Union of India
Citation: (1980) 3 SCC 625
Article: 368]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: A limited amending power is itself one of the basic features of the Constitution; Parliament cannot use its limited constituent power under Article 368 to enlarge that very power into an absolute, unlimited one.

HOLDING: Clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 (inserted by the 42nd Amendment) seeking to exclude judicial review and claim unlimited amending power are unconstitutional and void.

COURT REASONING: Chief Justice Y.V. Chandrachud observed that the donor of a limited power cannot expand that power into an absolute one. If by constitutional amendment Parliament could remove all limitations on its amending power, it would destroy the basic structure by claiming supreme sovereignty over the Constitution itself.

title: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India [Ratio 02: Harmonious Balance of FRs and DPSPs]
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: Harmonious balance, Fundamental Rights vs Directive Principles, bed-rock of Constitution
content:
[Case: Minerva Mills Ltd. v Union of India
Citation: (1980) 3 SCC 625
Article: 368]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: The harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) is an essential feature of the Basic Structure of the Indian Constitution.

HOLDING: Section 4 of the 42nd Amendment, which amended Article 31C to give blanket primacy to all Directive Principles over Articles 14 and 19, was declared unconstitutional.

COURT REASONING: The court held that Part III and Part IV together constitute the core of constitutional human rights. To destroy the guarantees of Fundamental Rights in the name of implementing Directive Principles is to uproot the foundation of the Constitution. They are like two wheels of a chariot; giving absolute supremacy to one at the expense of the other destroys the constitutional equilibrium.

title: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu [Ratio 01: Dynamic Anti-Arbitrariness Doctrine]
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: Dynamic equality, anti-arbitrariness, rule of law vs whim and caprice
content:
[Case: E.P. Royappa v State of Tamil Nadu
Citation: (1974) 4 SCC 3
Article: 14]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: Equality under Article 14 is a dynamic, living concept that cannot be confined within traditional classification doctrines; equality is completely antithetical to arbitrariness.

HOLDING: State action that is arbitrary, whimsical, or devoid of reason violates Article 14 per se, because equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies.

COURT REASONING: Justice P.N. Bhagwati propounded that traditional classification theory is merely a judicial formula for determining whether an enactment is arbitrary. Where an executive or legislative action fails the test of reason and fair play, it necessarily infringes the constitutional guarantee of equality under Article 14.

title: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India [Ratio 01: 50% Ceiling and Creamy Layer]
bench: 9-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: 50% reservation ceiling, creamy layer exclusion, substantive equality
content:
[Case: Indra Sawhney v Union of India
Citation: AIR 1993 SC 477
Article: 16]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: Reservations under Article 16(4) cannot exceed the strict 50% ceiling limit in any given year, and the 'Creamy Layer' must be excluded from OBC benefits to protect genuinely backward individuals.

HOLDING: 27% quota for OBCs is constitutionally valid subject to mandatory exclusion of the creamy layer and observance of the 50% cap on total reservations.

COURT REASONING: The 9-Judge Bench reasoned that Article 16(4) is an instrument of substantive equality under Article 16(1). However, reservation cannot become the rule and merit the exception; the 50% ceiling ensures administrative efficiency under Article 335 and fair competition for all citizens.

title: Shayara Bano v. Union of India [Ratio 01: Manifest Arbitrariness Doctrine]
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: Manifest arbitrariness, striking down legislation under Article 14, capricious state action
content:
[Case: Shayara Bano v Union of India
Citation: (2017) 9 SCC 1
Article: 14]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: Plenary legislation, statutory provisions, and subordinate laws can be struck down under Article 14 on the ground of 'Manifest Arbitrariness'.

HOLDING: Enactments or recognized legal practices that are irrational, capricious, disproportionate, or devoid of determining principle violate Article 14.

COURT REASONING: Justice R.F. Nariman clarified that manifest arbitrariness is an independent ground of constitutional invalidation. An action is manifestly arbitrary when it is done without adequate determining principle, or is capricious, irrational, or excessively disproportionate.

title: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India [Ratio 01: Constitutional Morality & Section 377]
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: Constitutional morality, decriminalization of Section 377 IPC, sexual orientation, dignity
content:
[Case: Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India
Citation: (2018) 10 SCC 1
Article: 21]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: 'Constitutional Morality' must prevail over majoritarian public morality; criminalizing consensual adult intimate relations under Section 377 IPC violates fundamental rights to liberty, dignity, and equality.

HOLDING: Consensual sexual acts between adults of the same sex are fully protected under Article 21 privacy and personal autonomy; Section 377 IPC is partially struck down.

COURT REASONING: The court held that the Constitution protects minorities against majoritarian prejudices. Sexual orientation is an innate, core attribute of human identity, and any statutory discrimination based on sexual orientation violates Article 14 and Article 15(1).

title: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India [Ratio 01: Discussion vs Advocacy vs Incitement]
bench: 2-Judge Bench
legal_topics: Section 66A IT Act struck down, freedom of speech online, incitement threshold, chilling effect
content:
[Case: Shreya Singhal v Union of India
Citation: (2015) 5 SCC 1
Article: 19]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: Freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) protects discussion and advocacy; state prohibition is permitted under Article 19(2) only when speech reaches the clear threshold of 'Incitement'.

HOLDING: Section 66A of the Information Technology Act was struck down in its entirety for unconstitutional vagueness, overbreadth, and creating an intolerable chilling effect on online expression.

COURT REASONING: Justice Nariman established the clear boundary in free speech jurisprudence: Discussion of unpopular ideas is protected; Advocacy of even radical causes is protected; only when advocacy crosses into direct Incitement to violence or public disorder can the State intervene under Article 19(2).

title: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation [Ratio 01: Right to Livelihood]
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: Right to livelihood, pavement dwellers, eviction safeguards, natural justice
content:
[Case: Olga Tellis v Bombay Municipal Corporation
Citation: (1985) 3 SCC 545
Article: 21]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: The Right to Livelihood is an integral and inseparable facet of the Right to Life under Article 21; deprivation of livelihood strips life of its meaningful existence.

HOLDING: State authorities cannot summarily evict slum and pavement dwellers without complying with basic requirements of procedural fairness, prior notice, and opportunity of representation.

COURT REASONING: Chief Justice Chandrachud reasoned that what makes life worth living is the means to sustain it. Depriving an impoverished citizen of their small pavement trade or dwelling inevitably deprives them of their means of survival, directly engaging Article 21.

title: Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, UT of Delhi [Ratio 01: Human Dignity]
bench: 2-Judge Bench
legal_topics: Right to life with dignity, beyond animal existence, prisoners' rights, access to lawyer
content:
[Case: Francis Coralie Mullin v Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi
Citation: (1981) 1 SCC 608
Article: 21]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: The Right to Life under Article 21 means the Right to Live with Human Dignity, extending far beyond mere physical animal survival to include basic necessities, culture, and social interaction.

HOLDING: Incarcerated individuals and preventive detenus retain the fundamental right to human dignity, including the right to freely consult legal counsel and meet family members without arbitrary restrictions.

COURT REASONING: Justice Bhagwati held that any act which damages, degrades, or diminishes human dignity strikes at the core of Article 21. Imprisonment curtails liberty of movement, but does not extinguish a human being's fundamental right to be treated with dignity.

title: Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar [Ratio 01: Speedy Trial & Legal Aid]
bench: 3-Judge Bench
legal_topics: Right to speedy trial, undertrials, free legal aid, bail reforms
content:
[Case: Hussainara Khatoon v State of Bihar
Citation: (1979) 3 SCC 816
Article: 21]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: The Right to a Speedy Trial and Free Legal Aid for indigent accused are constitutional fundamental rights implicit in Article 21 and Article 39A.

HOLDING: Prolonged, indefinite incarceration of undertrials without trial violates Article 21; State cannot plead financial or administrative inability to deny speedy trials or legal counsel.

COURT REASONING: Justice Bhagwati held that a criminal procedure which permits an accused person to languish in jail for years without trial is oppressive and fails the Maneka Gandhi test of being 'just, fair, and reasonable'. Free legal services to impoverished accused are an imperative constitutional duty of the State.

title: Selvi v. State of Karnataka [Ratio 01: Mental Privacy & Self-Incrimination]
bench: 3-Judge Bench
legal_topics: Narco-analysis, polygraph, self-incrimination under Article 20(3), mental privacy under Article 21
content:
[Case: Selvi v State of Karnataka
Citation: (2010) 7 SCC 263
Article: 20]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: Involuntary administration of neuro-scientific investigative techniques (narco-analysis, polygraph, brain electrical activation) violates protection against self-incrimination under Article 20(3) and mental privacy under Article 21.

HOLDING: Forcible extraction of subconscious information without consent is unconstitutional and inadmissible in criminal trials.

COURT REASONING: Chief Justice K.G. Balakrishnan held that Article 20(3) protects an accused's absolute right to choose between speech and silence. Forcible chemical or electrical intrusion into the human mind destroys mental privacy and bodily integrity, inflicting mental torture in violation of Article 21.

title: Common Cause v. Union of India [Ratio 01: Passive Euthanasia & Living Wills]
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: Passive euthanasia, right to die with dignity, living wills, advance medical directives
content:
[Case: Common Cause v Union of India
Citation: (2018) 5 SCC 1
Article: 21]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: The Fundamental Right to Life with dignity under Article 21 includes the right to a dignified dying process; passive euthanasia and Advance Medical Directives (Living Wills) are legally valid.

HOLDING: Withdrawing life support from terminally ill patients in irreversible vegetative state is constitutionally permissible under medical board supervision.

COURT REASONING: Chief Justice Dipak Misra affirmed that bodily autonomy and dignity belong to an individual until death. Forcing a dying person to undergo artificial and painful medical prolongation of dying against their express advance will violates human dignity under Article 21.

title: PUCL v. Union of India [Ratio 01: Telephone Tapping Safeguards]
bench: 2-Judge Bench
legal_topics: Telephone tapping, right to privacy, public emergency requirement, procedural safeguards
content:
[Case: PUCL v Union of India (Telephone Tapping)
Citation: (1997) 1 SCC 301
Article: 21]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: Interception of telephone conversations violates the Right to Privacy under Article 21 and Freedom of Expression under Article 19(1)(a) unless strictly justified by public emergency or public safety.

HOLDING: Tapping orders must be authorized exclusively by the Union/State Home Secretary and reviewed periodically by a High-Powered Committee.

COURT REASONING: The court observed that telephone conversations are private communications. Unregulated, secret interception by state intelligence agencies creates a pervasive state of fear and violates democratic liberties under Part III.

title: ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla [Ratio 01: Justice H.R. Khanna Dissent]
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: Habeas corpus during emergency, rule of law, inalienability of life and liberty, HR Khanna dissent
content:
[Case: ADM Jabalpur v Shivkant Shukla
Citation: (1976) 2 SCC 521
Article: 21]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: Even during a proclaimed Emergency under Article 352, the State possesses no constitutional or legal authority to deprive a citizen of life or personal liberty without authority of valid law.

HOLDING: Justice H.R. Khanna's dissent established that the Rule of Law is the supreme command of the Constitution; presidential orders under Article 359 cannot immunize illegal, arbitrary detentions from judicial inquiry.

COURT REASONING: Justice Khanna declared that Article 21 did not create the right to life; life and liberty are natural, inalienable human rights. Without the Rule of Law, a civilized society collapses into executive lawlessness. His dissent was officially adopted by Parliament in the 44th Amendment and unanimously affirmed by the 9-Judge Bench in Puttaswamy (2017).

title: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu [Ratio 01: Ninth Schedule Subject to Basic Structure]
bench: 9-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: Ninth Schedule, basic structure touchstone, judicial review of constitutional amendments
content:
[Case: I.R. Coelho v State of Tamil Nadu
Citation: (2007) 2 SCC 1
Article: 368]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: All statutes placed in the Ninth Schedule on or after April 24, 1973 must pass the constitutional test of the Basic Structure Doctrine; Parliament cannot use Article 31B to create an untouchable legislative sanctuary.

HOLDING: Any Ninth Schedule law that abrogates the golden triangle (Articles 14, 19, 21) or destroys the basic features of the Constitution will be invalidated by courts.

COURT REASONING: Chief Justice Sabharwal held that constituent power cannot be delegated to ordinary statutes placed in the Ninth Schedule. The 'rights test' and 'essence of rights test' apply to prevent Parliament from eroding constitutional supremacy through the device of the Ninth Schedule.

title: R.C. Cooper v. Union of India [Ratio 01: Direct and Inevitable Effect Test]
bench: 11-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: Direct and inevitable effect test, dismantling Gopalan silos, bank nationalization
content:
[Case: R.C. Cooper v Union of India
Citation: (1970) 1 SCC 248
Article: 14]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: The constitutional validity of state action is determined by its direct operation and inevitable effect upon fundamental rights, not by the legislative object or form of the statute.

HOLDING: Overruled the Gopalan doctrine of mutually exclusive fundamental rights; laws affecting property or personal liberty must satisfy both Article 14 equality and Article 19 reasonableness.

COURT REASONING: Justice J.C. Shah held that state action impairs constitutional rights when its inevitable consequence restricts those rights. The court must look at the substantive impact upon the citizen rather than the formal legislative label under which the law was enacted.

title: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India [Ratio 01: Internet as Fundamental Right & Proportionality]
bench: 3-Judge Bench
legal_topics: Internet shutdown, fundamental rights via internet, proportionality standard, publishing orders
content:
[Case: Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India
Citation: (2020) 3 SCC 637
Article: 19]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: Freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) and the right to carry on trade/profession under Article 19(1)(g) over the medium of the internet are constitutionally protected fundamental rights; indefinite internet shutdowns are illegal.

HOLDING: Any internet suspension must adhere to the four-fold proportionality test, be strictly temporary, and all suspension orders must be published for judicial scrutiny.

COURT REASONING: The Supreme Court observed that the internet has become an indispensable modern vehicle for expressing thought, commerce, education, and access to justice. An indefinite shutdown creates a complete prohibition rather than a reasonable restriction, breaching the doctrine of proportionality.

title: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India [Ratio 01: Judicial Review is Basic Structure]
bench: 7-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: Judicial review, basic structure, administrative tribunals, High Court supervisory writ jurisdiction
content:
[Case: L. Chandra Kumar v Union of India
Citation: (1997) 3 SCC 261
Article: 32]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: The power of judicial review vested in the High Courts under Articles 226/227 and in the Supreme Court under Article 32 is an inviolable basic feature of the Constitution that cannot be ousted by legislative enactment.

HOLDING: Statutory provisions excluding High Court writ jurisdiction over Administrative Tribunals are unconstitutional; all tribunal orders are subject to review by a Division Bench of the High Court.

COURT REASONING: The 7-Judge Bench held that tribunals can serve as courts of first instance, but they can never substitute the constitutional writ jurisdiction of the High Courts. The constitutional oversight of higher judiciary is indispensable for maintaining the rule of law.

title: Indian Young Lawyers Assn v. State of Kerala [Ratio 01: Biological Exclusion & Constitutional Morality]
bench: 5-Judge Constitution Bench
legal_topics: Sabarimala entry, biological exclusion of women, constitutional morality over social custom, untouchability
content:
[Case: Indian Young Lawyers Association v State of Kerala (Sabarimala)
Citation: (2019) 11 SCC 1
Article: 25]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: Excluding women from public religious worship based on biological physiological factors violates equality under Article 14, non-discrimination under Article 15, and personal dignity under Article 21; Constitutional Morality supersedes patriarchal custom.

HOLDING: Rule 3(b) of the Kerala Entry Rules barring women aged 10-50 from Sabarimala temple was struck down as unconstitutional.

COURT REASONING: Chief Justice Dipak Misra and Justice Chandrachud held that religious freedom under Article 25(1) is subject to fundamental rights. Equating menstruation with physiological impurity is a form of untouchability violating Article 17. The Constitution rejects religious patriarchies that subordinate women.

title: NALSA v. Union of India [Ratio 01: Gender Identity Self-Determination]
bench: 2-Judge Bench
legal_topics: Third gender recognition, transgender rights, gender self-determination, bodily autonomy
content:
[Case: National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) v Union of India
Citation: (2014) 5 SCC 438
Article: 21]

LEGAL PRINCIPLE: Self-determination of one's gender identity is an inalienable component of personal liberty, dignity, and autonomy guaranteed under Article 21; discrimination based on gender identity violates Articles 14, 15, and 16.

HOLDING: Transgender persons have the constitutional right to self-identify their gender as male, female, or third gender without undergoing sex reassignment surgery.

COURT REASONING: Justice K.S. Radhakrishnan held that gender identity lies at the core of human personality. The binary classification of male and female fails to accommodate persons of diverse gender expressions, depriving them of equal citizenship and fundamental dignity.
